articles.title: Intruder shoots teacher dead inside UP school, kills himself
articles.summary: Teacher Nishat Fatima shot dead by intruder at Lakhimpur Kheri private school; attacker Saud Ansari later killed himself; police probe entry, CCTV, motive.
articles.body: MEERUT: A 26-year-old woman teacher was shot dead inside a private school in Lakhimpur Kheri on Monday by a 28-year-old man who entered the campus carrying a country-made pistol and later shot himself, triggering panic among around 350 students present at the time.The attack came barely seven weeks after a private-school teacher in Faridabad was stabbed repeatedly inside her campus by a man who had entered seeking her out.Police identified the victim as Nishat Fatima, a resident of Hidayat Nagar, and the attacker as Saud Ansari, 28, of Naurangabad.SSP Kheri Khyati Garg said Ansari reached Children’s Academy in Shahpura Kothi area around 11.30am, met Fatima and went upstairs with her before an argument broke out.“He took out a country-made pistol and fired three rounds at her at close range. He then shot himself. Both died on the spot,” Garg told TOI. Police said Fatima suffered fatal injuries to her head and upper body.Gunshots sent students and staff running for safety while examinations were under way.School management alerted police, who moved children away from the crime scene, cordoned off the corridor and called forensic teams. Investigators recovered four spent cartridges, one live cartridge and the country-made pistol.Police are now examining how Ansari entered the campus with a firearm, his movements inside the two-storey building and security arrangements at the school, including CCTV coverage and visitor-entry procedures.SSP added, “The accused had been forcing the victim to marry, as alleged by the woman’s family in the complaint. The victim’s brother, Shadab Akhter, has filed a complaint, following which an FIR has been filed against the accused Ansari under BNS section 103 (murder) and section 61(2) (criminal conspiracy) against Ansari’s parents. Shadab alleged that they had informed the parents that their son was harassing Fatima, but they didn’t take any action and, at their behest, he committed the crime.”Ansari’s social media posts in the days before the shooting have also become part of the investigation. He had posted photographs with messages such as “Usse Bhool Ja” and, shortly before the attack, uploaded a longer note asking people to delete his photographs and messages after his death. “In this world nothing is permanent, no one is permanent. We came in this world so we have to leave this world for sure,” part of the post read.The incident echoed the Aug 3 Faridabad school killing, when a masked 21-year-old man entered a private school in Sikrona, sought out teacher Sandhya Karhana and stabbed her more than 30 times in roughly 30 seconds after dragging her from the classroom area. The attack, captured on CCTV, had similarly raised questions over how an armed outsider could enter a school and reach a teacher during working hours.Stay updated with the latest Bareilly news. articles.title: Yavatmal in shock, IIT-Bombay student’s kin seek CID probe; allege boy’s death was not suicide
articles.summary: IIT Bombay student Sahil Wakode, 19, found dead in hostel; Yavatmal family rejects suicide theory, alleges foul play, seeks CID probe, claims harassment.
articles.body: YAVATMAL: The family of 19-year-old Sahil Ravindra Wakode, a second-year student at IIT Bombay, has demanded a CID investigation into his death at the institute hostel, alleging that the incident was not a suicide.Wakode’s family alleged foul play and submitted a letter to the district administration in Yavatmal seeking a probe. While his parents have left for Mumbai to follow up on the case, relatives back home set up banners outside the family’s home demanding justice for Sahil.His aunt Ganga Wakode rejected the suicide theory. “Sahil could never have taken his life,” she said. Ganga said Sahil was intelligent, focused and composed since childhood and committed to his academic goals, making it difficult for them to accept that he would take such a drastic step.Ganga also questioned the institute’s handling of an alleged mobile phone incident during an examination, asking how Sahil could have used a phone inside an IIT hall where phones are prohibited. The family said the institute should have informed his parents had any such incident occurred.The family’s allegations of caste-based discrimination, psychological pressure or humiliating treatment at the institute have not been independently established. No response from IIT Bombay or the district administration on the CID demand was available.Sahil, a second-year student from Shelu Brahmanwada village in Arni taluka, scored 94 percentile in JEE Advanced, ranking 614th nationally in the Scheduled Caste category. articles.summary: Interdição em cruzamento começou a gerar congestionamento pela manhã. Motoristas começaram a furar o bloqueio no início da tarde.
articles.body:
O trânsito na avenida Gentil Bittencourt, uma das principais vias de Belém , registrou lentidão e pontos de congestionamento nesta quarta-feira (13). O motivo é uma interdição para a realização de uma obra de saneamento e drenagem no cruzamento com a travessa Guerra Passos, no bairro de Canudos.

A interdição da pista começou na Gentil Bittencourt a partir da Travessa Barão de Mamoré (para quem segue no sentido Terra Firme). No entanto, o desrespeito à sinalização por parte dos motoristas transformou o local em um ponto de perigo.

Pela manhã, carros e motocicletas foram flagrados furando o bloqueio físico e passando pela área isolada como se a via estivesse liberada. No trecho, havia presença de operários e maquinário pesado.

Com o início dos trabalhos, os próprios operários da obra precisaram se posicionar no ponto de bloqueio na Guerra Passos para impedir fisicamente a passagem dos veículos.

Motociclistas ainda foram flagrados utilizando passarelas de pedestres sobre o canal para desviar da interdição.

articles.title: Apagão em Viracopos: Azul cancela 26 voos e registra atrasos hoje | G1
articles.standfirst: Companhia confirmou cancelamentos por causa da falta de energia no aeroporto. Gerador falhou durante interrupção, segundo terminal.
articles.summary: O apagão em Viracopos causou o cancelamento de 26 voos da Azul e dezenas de atrasos nesta terça-feira, afetando a operação do aeroporto por até dois dias.
articles.body:
O apagão que atingiu o Aeroporto Internacional de Viracopos , em Campinas (SP), nesta terça-feira (22), provocou o cancelamento de pelo menos 26 voos da Azul, segundo a companhia aérea.

Dados da plataforma Flightradar24 apontavam, às 13h06, 81 voos atrasados e 26 cancelamentos.

A Azul confirmou que os 26 cancelamentos ocorreram em razão da queda de energia. Já no caso dos atrasos registrados pela plataforma, não há confirmação de que todos estejam relacionados ao apagão.

Viracopos , principal base de operações da Azul, informou que os efeitos da ocorrência sobre a malha aérea podem se estender por até dois dias.

A falta de energia começou por volta das 3h10 e atingiu uma das subestações responsáveis pelo abastecimento do saguão de check-in. O problema também afetou equipamentos usados no embarque e provocou filas no terminal.

Segundo a concessionária Aeroportos Brasil Viracopos, o aeroporto possui um gerador para situações de emergência, mas o equipamento não funcionou durante o apagão . A administradora apura o motivo da falha.

Também houve uma interrupção na ligação entre três pontos de redundância do sistema elétrico do terminal, que deveriam evitar a perda de energia.

A Azul informou que acompanha a situação junto às equipes responsáveis pelo aeroporto e adota medidas para reduzir os impactos aos passageiros com origem, destino ou conexão em Viracopos.

A companhia orientou os clientes a consultar o status da reserva nos canais oficiais antes de se dirigir ao aeroporto e afirmou que os passageiros afetados recebem a assistência prevista na Resolução 400 da Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil (Anac).

Mais cedo, antes de confirmar os cancelamentos provocados pela queda de energia, a Azul havia atribuído impactos na operação a condições meteorológicas na região de Campinas.

A concessionária de Viracopos informou que os passageiros continuavam conseguindo embarcar, mas com um processo mais lento.

A Latam informou que registrou atraso em um voo com destino a Brasília (DF). A aeronave decolou às 7h04, com 1h24 de atraso.

Já a Gol afirmou que tinha apenas um voo previsto para decolar de Viracopos durante a manhã e que a operação foi realizada.

Falta de energia provoca filas e afeta embarque no Aeroporto de Viracopos — Foto: Wanderson Ramon

A CPFL Paulista informou que o sistema elétrico responsável pelo abastecimento de Viracopos operava normalmente e que não houve registro de falha na rede da distribuidora.

Segundo a empresa, o problema teve origem nas instalações internas do aeroporto .

Durante o apagão, os painéis de informações sobre os voos ficaram fora do ar durante a madrugada e o início da manhã. Os equipamentos de raio-X usados no acesso à área de embarque também foram afetados, e parte dos procedimentos de segurança precisou ser realizada manualmente.

As filas para acessar a área de embarque se estenderam pelo saguão, enquanto passageiros também enfrentaram espera nos balcões de check-in e despacho de bagagens.

As áreas de pátio, a pista de pousos e decolagens e as vias de acesso ao aeroporto não foram afetadas pela interrupção, segundo Viracopos.

Filas para despacho de bagagem no Aeroporto de Viracopos, em Campinas, na manhã desta terça-feira (22) — Foto: Jorge Talmon/EPTV

"São Paulo, 22 de setembro de 2026 - Devido à ocorrência de queda de energia no Aeroporto Internacional de Viracopos, em Campinas (SP), a Azul está com sua operação impactada no terminal. Até o momento, 26 voos foram cancelados, além de registros de atrasos. A Companhia acompanha a situação junto às equipes responsáveis pelo aeroporto e adota as medidas necessárias para minimizar os impactos aos Clientes com voos de origem, destino e conexões em Viracopos.

A empresa orienta que os Clientes com voos impactados verifiquem o status de sua reserva nos canais oficiais da Companhia antes de se dirigir ao aeroporto.

Os Clientes estão recebendo a assistência prevista na Resolução 400 da Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil (Anac). A Azul ressalta que medidas operacionais são adotadas sempre com foco na segurança de suas operações, valor primordial para a Companhia".

articles.body: NEW DELHI: A 34-year-old man was arrested after local residents allegedly caught him sexually assaulting a six-year-old girl in central Delhi’s Kishanganj area on Monday evening, police said.The accused, identified as Ankit, a resident of Kishanganj, was apprehended by local residents and handed over to police. Enraged locals allegedly thrashed Ankit and his mother outside the police station, following which police intervened and dispersed the crowd.The child was immediately taken for a medical examination, while police inspected the spot where the alleged incident took place and collected evidence. An FIR under relevant provisions of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) was being registered, police said.Police said statements of the child and other people aware of the incident would be recorded and the medical examination report would form part of the investigation. The circumstances leading to the alleged incident and the exact sequence of events are being investigated.The incident comes amid a spate of cases involving alleged sexual offences against minors in Delhi.On September 21, a 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped by three men posing as policemen at a park near Kalkaji Mandir. On September 16, a minor girl was allegedly sexually assaulted by a 56-year-old man inside a shop in Sadar Bazaar. articles.title: Archaeologists found 500 Iron Age iron bars in Austria’s Danube, revealing a 1-tonne cargo transported 2,000 years ago
articles.summary: Europe News: Archaeologists have identified at least 500 forged iron bars recovered from the Danube in Upper Austria as the largest known assemblage of Iron Age ir.
articles.body: Archaeologists have identified at least 500 forged iron bars recovered from the Danube in Upper Austria as the largest known assemblage of Iron Age iron in Europe. The discovery was made in 2019 during gravel extraction at Deinham, when workers found double-pointed iron objects in material taken from beneath the river’s water level. According to a research article published by Cambridge University Press titled ‘A sunken ship cargo of 500 bipyramidal bars? Implications for La Tène period iron production and trade along the Danube’, states that radiocarbon dating of three bars places the assemblage in the Late Iron Age, with dates falling between the fourth and first centuries BC.How the 500 iron bars were discovered at DeinhamWorkers at a gravel extraction site in Deinham identified at least 500 iron bars after discovering numerous double-pointed objects in 2019. The material had been removed from beneath the Danube’s water level, which disturbed and destroyed the original archaeological context. The finds were brought to the attention of the Federal Monuments Office, which was followed by the hand collection of additional pieces from the gravel heaps.A total of 540 fragments were recovered. From the material, researchers identified a minimum of 500 individual bars. Many of the bars are heavily corroded, while sand and gravel remain attached to their surfaces. In 2023, the recovered finds were donated to the Oberösterreichische Landes-Kultur GmbH in Linz, where they are now kept in permanent storage.What did radiocarbon dating reveal about the iron barsThe Deinham bars date to a later period than earlier examples of bipyramidal iron products. Researchers radiocarbon-dated samples from three bars, producing two probability peaks. One falls in the second half of the fourth century BC, while the other extends from the end of the third century into the second century BC. The later date range is consistent with archaeological evidence from comparable BLD6 bars.Based on their form and dating, the researchers classify the Deinham pieces as a new BLD6 variant of forged iron semi-products rather than cast ingots. Most complete bars are elongated and double-pointed, measuring an average of 285mm in length. They weigh an average of 2,070g, with individual complete bars ranging from 959g to 3,824g.How were the iron bars transported along the DanubeThe location of the finding provides clues about how the iron bars may have been transported. The bars were recovered from silted-up channels along the right bank of the Danube, near the entrance to the Eferding Basin. Similar iron-bar finds from Central European rivers are generally interpreted as cargo lost during transport or in shipwrecks.The researchers do not completely rule out deliberate deposition, but note that the uniform composition of the Deinham assemblage differs from more varied ritual deposits found in rivers. No remains of a boat were found with the bars, as the original archaeological context was disturbed during gravel extraction. The study considers river transport the most likely explanation and notes that Late Iron Age logboats could carry more than one tonne of cargo.How large was the Iron Age iron cargo found at DeinhamThe Deinham assemblage has an estimated total weight of 1,035kg, making it the largest known assemblage of Iron Age iron bars in Europe. The researchers say its combined weight provides evidence of the scale of iron production during the third and second centuries BC. They estimate that one tonne of iron could have produced about 500 swords, allowing for manufacturing losses, or around 8,000 nails. The researchers also indicate that the cargo may have originated further upstream, with the Manching, Kelheim and Upper Palatinate region considered the most plausible production area.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: UK backs Saudi Arabia with RAF Voyager refuelling support amid Houthi campaign
articles.summary: UK News: The UK has stated that it will provide Saudi Arabia with defensive military support, including air-to-air refuelling for Saudi fighter jets, as Riyadh.
articles.body: The UK has stated that it will provide Saudi Arabia with defensive military support, including air-to-air refuelling for Saudi fighter jets, as Riyadh faces a renewed campaign of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen.Prime minister Andy Burnham said Saudi Arabia had requested military support and that Britain had agreed to provide an RAF Voyager aircraft to refuel Saudi jets for several weeks.The aircraft is expected to operate from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. British officials described the deployment as “time limited” and said it was intended to help Saudi Arabia defend its energy infrastructure and keep key oil routes open.The move comes as the Houthis have advanced along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and taken control of the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, a major maritime route connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.UK links support to energy securityBurnham said the decision was partly driven by concerns over the impact of the conflict on energy supplies and the cost of living in Britain.“I go back to the point I made about cost-of-living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region,” Burnham told reporters from BBC.Saudi Arabia has faced a series of Houthi attacks in recent days, including missile and drone strikes targeting Riyadh and energy infrastructure along the Red Sea coast. The attacks have raised concerns over further disruption to Saudi oil exports.The UK already provides air-defence support to Saudi Arabia, including the deployment of the Sky Sabre system. The new refuelling mission will allow Saudi aircraft to remain airborne for longer while responding to incoming threats.Britain stops short of direct strikesThe deployment is significantly more limited than Britain's previous military action against the Houthis.In January 2024, the UK joined the US in carrying out airstrikes against Houthi military targets in Yemen after the group attacked commercial shipping in the Red Sea. Further British-American strikes followed later that year.This time, the UK has framed its involvement as defensive support rather than direct attacks on Houthi positions.The announcement also comes as Burnham prepares for his first face-to-face meeting with US President Donald Trump at the UN. Burnham said he would urge Trump to work towards ending the war in Iran, arguing that the conflict and the wider instability in the Middle East were contributing to economic pressure in Britain.The UK government is also concerned about the wider consequences of the fighting for global energy and shipping routes. The Bab al-Mandab Strait has become a new flashpoint after the Houthis' recent advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast, while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted.Burnham said Britain wanted to see the conflict end as quickly as possible and was ready to work with its allies to reduce the wider instability.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: An elderly tenant in Melbourne refused a $65-a-week rent increase and kept paying her old rent; tribunal later struck down her eviction notice
articles.summary: Rest of World News: An elderly social housing tenant in Melbourne has had her eviction notice struck out after she continued paying her previous rent despite a weekly inc.
articles.body: An elderly social housing tenant in Melbourne has had her eviction notice struck out after she continued paying her previous rent despite a weekly increase of about $65. The dispute began after HousingFirst took over several properties previously run by Glenloch. The tenant challenged whether the higher rent had been properly introduced and kept paying about $234 a week. According to ABC News, the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal(VCAT) later found the eviction notice invalid because of confusion over the amount the tenant was said to owe.Why the elderly Melbourne tenant refused the rent increaseThe renter was one of several elderly residents affected after HousingFirst took over a group of inner-east Melbourne properties in 2023. The homes had previously been operated under a private trust known as Glenloch, according to ABC News.HousingFirst later increased the rents for residents of those properties. The organisation said the changes were needed because the homes had previously been subject to low and inconsistent rents. It said the increases were intended to bring the properties into line with the rest of its community housing portfolio while limiting the effect on tenants.For the elderly renter at the centre of the tribunal case, the proposed increase was about $65 each week. Instead of accepting the new amount, she continued paying the roughly $234 weekly rent she had been paying before.The disagreement was not simply about whether she could afford the additional money. It also concerned whether HousingFirst had followed the correct process when increasing the rent.The rent dispute turned into an eviction caseThe situation became more serious in April 2026, when HousingFirst issued the tenant with a notice to vacate. The organisation argued that she owed more than $1,000 in unpaid rent because she had continued paying the old amount.The dispute was then taken to VCAT, where both sides presented their positions. ABC News reported that the parties had attempted to negotiate a payment plan, but the central disagreement remained whether the rent had actually been increased in a legally valid way.The tenant was represented by Shane McGrath from the Housing for the Aged Action Group. He told the tribunal that she believed a formal notice of rent increase was required. Because the elderly tenant did not consider the increase valid, she had continued paying her previous rent. Her representative argued that this meant she was not actually in arrears when the eviction notice was issued.The issue therefore became more complicated than a straightforward case of unpaid rent. It involved the validity of the increase itself and whether the amount claimed from the tenant was accurate.How did HousingFirst justified the higher rentHousingFirst took a different position on the matter. Its representative told the tribunal that the particular nature of the rent increase meant that notice periods that would normally apply were not required.The organisation also wanted the tribunal to determine whether the notice it had given was legal and enforceable. If the increase was found to be valid, its representative said HousingFirst wanted to establish a repayment arrangement with the tenant.The wider rent changes were part of an effort to bring the former Glenloch properties into line with HousingFirst's other community housing homes. ABC News reported that the organisation's community housing portfolio caps rent at 30% of household income. But the changes placed some elderly residents under greater financial pressure.Tribunal’s decision about the eviction noticeSenior VCAT member Vivienne Topp ultimately struck out the eviction notice, but the decision did not settle the underlying disagreement over whether the rent increase itself was valid.Instead, the tribunal focused on the amount stated on the notice to vacate. Topp found there was confusion surrounding how much the tenant was alleged to owe.The renter and her advocate had disputed the figure written on the notice. After hearing the evidence, Topp declared that the notice was not valid and struck out the matter.That distinction is important because the tribunal did not rule that HousingFirst's rent increase was unlawful. The eviction notice was rejected because of the confusion over the amount claimed as owing.What could happen next in this rent dispute matterABC News reported that it was unclear whether the matter would return to VCAT. The tribunal's decision dealt with the validity of the particular notice to vacate instead of providing a final ruling on the disputed rent increase.According to ABC News, HousingFirst manages more than 2,000 properties across Melbourne. The organisation began as the Port Phillip Housing Association before growing into a major social housing provider.For the tenant involved, however, the immediate issue was much more personal about whether continuing to pay the rent she believed was valid, would result in her losing the home.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: From Op Sindoor to Urgent Fury, how network warfare has changed the way conflicts are being fought
articles.summary: News News: Well entrenched in the information age, network-centric warfare is changing the way wars are fought. At its core, network-centric warfare is about gat.
articles.body: Well entrenched in the information age, network-centric warfare is changing the way wars are fought. At its core, network-centric warfare is about gathering and turning information into a battlefield advantage. This is done by connecting sensors, commanders and weapons into a single digital fabric that lets forces see, decide, act and strike faster than an adversary can react. Rather than relying on the rigid hierarchies associated with militaries, the new paradigm flattens command structures, linking soldiers, smart weapons, command centres and platforms across land, air, sea and space into one shared communication network, stretching from army headquarters down to the individual soldier on the ground.The nature of combat itself is evolving alongside this shift. Small drones have fundamentally changed how soldiers operate on the battlefield, acting as what one recent analysis called "bombs with eyes," capable of spotting, tracking and striking troops from considerable distances. This has forced a rethink in tactics, with soldiers increasingly prioritising concealment over holding ground, and a growing recognition that counter-drone technology, lasers, microwave weapons, interceptor drones, and anti-drone rifles need to extend down to individual soldier-level protection, not just larger area defences.For India, network-centric warfare is fast becoming a genuine security imperative. The country faces two very different border theatres, alongside pressure across maritime, air, space and cyber domains all at once. In such an environment, speed of information matters enormously, as a force that detects and understands a threat first only gains an advantage if that information can also be shared reliably and converted swiftly into action.India has already built meaningful pieces of this architecture. AFNET and the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) connect sensors, command centres and air defence systems, forming the digital backbone of the Air Force, while the Defence Communication Network (DCN) provides secure connectivity across all three services. Akashteer has further strengthened integration of Army air defence systems into this wider network. These systems proved their worth during Operation Sindoor, when IACCS, Akashteer and the Navy's Trigun system worked in tandem to build a shared operational picture and support faster battlefield decisions. India also rolled out the Indian Radio Software Architecture Standard 1.0 in October 2025, a common software framework enabling different military radios to communicate across platforms, reducing reliance on foreign communication technology in the process. Other networks, such as the Artillery Combat Command and Control System (ACCCS) network, also improve the effectiveness of this increasingly important arm.Ultimately, the decisive edge in network-centric warfare won't necessarily belong to whoever fields the most advanced individual platform, but to whoever can keep their network functioning under attack, make sound decisions under pressure, and deliver effects at precisely the right moment—a network that survives uncertainty rather than merely one that's fast. In India, companies like Bharat Electronics, Tata Advanced Systems, Zen Technologies and Hexagon R&D India are among those actively building toward this capability.

articles.title: Russia planning 'grey zone operations'? Why is Europe intuitively spooked
articles.summary: Europe News: What if Russia strikes Nato territory, but makes it look like an accident?That is the possibility now worrying Europe. Polish prime minister Donald Tu.
articles.body: What if Russia strikes Nato territory, but makes it look like an accident?That is the possibility now worrying Europe. Polish prime minister Donald Tusk has warned that Russia could strike Nato territory and make it appear accidental: what is considered a "deniable grey-zone operation".Britain has urged its citizens to keep tinned food and water at home, while Germany is readying hospitals for mass casualties.Even Switzerland, a country that has avoided military alliances for two centuries, has adopted a security strategy built around defending itself if attacked. None of this appears to be a coincidence. It reflects a shared, growing fear that Vladimir Putin may be preparing to test Nato somewhere beyond Ukraine's borders.The shadow warMuch of what worries Western officials is not a tank invasion but something harder to pin down. Drones drifting into Baltic airspace, sabotage at airports, cyberattacks, plots involving criminal networks operating far from Russia's own territory.Individually, each incident can be denied or dismissed as an accident but likely form a pattern that lets Moscow probe Nato's resolve without technically starting a war.One flashpoint that keeps coming up is the Suwałki Gap, a narrow strip of land barely 65 miles wide connecting Poland to the Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia.If that corridor were ever cut off, even briefly, it would sever the Baltics from the rest of the alliance and force a very uncomfortable question.Would all 32 Nato members actually go to war over such a small piece of territory, especially one that could reignite fears of nuclear escalation? Nobody in Washington, Berlin or Paris can promise a confident yes, and that uncertainty is precisely what Moscow may be trying to exploit.Watching the calendarRussia Duma elections, held from 18 to 20 September, are now behind it, and it has been widely believed the result was never in doubt given how tightly the process is controlled by the Kremlin. What matters more to European planners is what comes after. Domestic elections tend to absorb a regime's attention and resources.With that distraction removed, some officials fear Putin may feel freer to escalate pressure on Nato's eastern flank, whether through further drone incursions, sabotage, or a more deliberate military manoeuvre designed to test the alliance's unity.Lithuania's prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, has been unusually candid about the mood on the ground as he told the BBC his country has drawn up plans for a "variety of scenarios", including how to move elderly residents out of cities "smoothly" if the worst happened."We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us," Lithuania PM said.Lithuania borders the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and has already seen Nato jets scramble to shoot down a drone that entered its airspace, an incident Britain's defence secretary described by saying "we stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: US News: James Farthing, a Kentucky man who won a $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in April 2025, has been arrested for the fifth time since claiming the prize.
articles.body: James Farthing, a Kentucky man who won a $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in April 2025, has been arrested for the fifth time since claiming the prize. The latest arrest took place on September 20, 2026, after deputies reportedly found him asleep inside a running Ford Mustang in a Walmart car park in Georgetown. Authorities charged him with being intoxicated in a public place following reports of alcohol-related impairment. The incident adds to a series of legal cases involving Farthing since his jackpot win. He had shared the historic prize with his mother, Linda Grizzle, after purchasing a $2 ticket from a Georgetown retailer.Earlier incidents included an April 2025 arrest in Florida, where Farthing was accused of kicking a sheriff’s deputy during an altercation. He later pleaded guilty to misdemeanor battery and obstruction or resisting arrest. In February 2026, he faced an intimidation charge, followed by burglary and marijuana-possession charges in March after being accused of entering a Lexington home and stealing $12,000. In July, he was arrested on domestic violence-related charges, including first-degree strangulation and fourth-degree assault. Farthing has pleaded not guilty to the domestic violence charges.Police found Kentucky Powerball winner asleep in a running MustangThe latest incident began shortly before 3 a.m. on Sunday, September 20, when a caller reported a white Ford Mustang stopped in the middle of an intersection in Georgetown, Kentucky. The vehicle later moved to a Walmart car park on Osborne Way, according to the arrest citation reported by WKYT.Deputies arrived and found the Mustang parked near an electric vehicle charging station with its engine running. Farthing was reportedly asleep in the passenger seat. Officers knocked on the window several times before he woke up.The arrest citation described several signs of impairment, including the smell of alcohol and marijuana, bloodshot and watery eyes, slurred speech and difficulty maintaining balance. Farthing was subsequently charged with being intoxicated in a public place and taken to the Scott County Detention Center.According to the arrest report, Farthing told deputies that a woman had driven him to the car park and left him there. Authorities reviewed surveillance footage, which reportedly showed no one exiting the Mustang after it entered the car park.How James Farthing won Kentucky's record Powerball prizeFarthing purchased the winning Powerball ticket from Clark's Pump N Shop in Georgetown. The ticket matched the required numbers in the April 26, 2025 drawing, resulting in a $167.3 million jackpot.The Kentucky Lottery identified the prize as the largest Powerball jackpot ever won in the state. Farthing and his mother, Linda Grizzle, claimed the winnings together and announced that they would share the fortune.The win brought significant attention to the family, while Farthing later appeared in news reports concerning several encounters with law enforcement in Kentucky and Florida.Florida arrest came shortly after the jackpot winFarthing's first reported arrest after winning the lottery took place in Florida in April 2025. Authorities accused him of battery involving a law enforcement officer and resisting arrest following an incident at a hotel.According to the Associated Press, officers said Farthing kicked a deputy in the face during an altercation and attempted to flee. He faced charges connected to the confrontation.The Independent later reported that Farthing pleaded guilty in the case and received a sentence of time served and $1,000 in fines.February arrest involved an intimidation chargeIn February 2026, Farthing was arrested in Georgetown on a charge involving intimidation of a participant in a legal process. The case followed a report from a woman who contacted emergency services and said she feared for her safety.According to People, police investigated an incident at Farthing's home and reportedly found a woman hiding under a desk. Authorities also searched the property and allegedly discovered a handgun, ammunition, marijuana and drug paraphernalia.Burglary and marijuana charges followed in MarchFarthing faced additional charges in March 2026 in connection with allegations of burglary and marijuana possession. Authorities accused him of entering a Lexington home and stealing approximately $12,000 in cash.The Guardian reported that investigators used security camera footage during the investigation. Farthing was later reportedly located at a casino.Local news reports said the burglary and marijuana charges were dismissed in May. The dismissal applied to those specific charges and did not resolve his other legal cases.July domestic violence case involved strangulation allegationsIn late July 2026, Farthing was charged with first-degree strangulation and fourth-degree assault following a reported domestic violence incident in Scott County.Police said a woman reported that a verbal argument became physical after a boating trip. According to the arrest report, she alleged that Farthing placed both hands around her neck and restricted her breathing. Authorities also reported visible marks on her neck.Farthing pleaded not guilty through his legal representative. A judge set his bond at $15,000 and ordered him to avoid contact with the alleged victim. He was also required to wear an electronic monitoring device with a notification feature.Fifth arrest adds to Farthing's legal casesThe September arrest is the fifth reported arrest involving Farthing since he won the Kentucky Powerball jackpot in 2025.The latest case concerns public intoxication in Scott County and follows the July domestic violence-related arrest. His legal proceedings remain separate from the lottery win, which he shared with his mother.The public intoxication case is pending in Scott County District Court, with an arraignment reportedly scheduled for Tuesday, September 22, 2026.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: China expanded planted forests by about 35,000 sq km; 20 years of data show carbon uptake began declining within 15 years in 80% of areas
articles.summary: China News: China's Yellow River Basin has gained roughly 35,000 square kilometres of planted forest over the past three decades, but a study of nearly 20 years o.
articles.body: China's Yellow River Basin has gained roughly 35,000 square kilometres of planted forest over the past three decades, but a study of nearly 20 years of monitoring data suggests some of those forests begin losing their carbon-sequestration momentum far earlier than their expected maturity. Research published in Scientific Reports titled Analysis of 20 years of monitoring data reveals insufficient carbon sequestration potential of planted forests in dryland regions found that annual net primary productivity, a measure used to assess vegetation carbon fixation, shifted from increasing to declining within 15 years of planting in more than 80% of the areas where planted forests expanded. In nearly half of those areas, the decline began within 10 years. The finding comes from an analysis of the Yellow River Basin between 2001 and 2019, using annual net primary productivity and soil organic carbon datasets alongside land-cover and climate data. The researchers say increasing drought and limited water availability are among the factors restricting the long-term carbon gains of afforestation in this dryland region.Forest expansion brought an early boost to carbon uptakeThe Yellow River Basin has been the focus of extensive ecological restoration since the 1990s, including large-scale afforestation programmes intended to reduce land degradation and improve ecosystem functioning. More than half of the basin receives less than 400mm of annual precipitation, however, leaving many areas with limited water availability for sustained vegetation growth. The researchers examined net primary productivity (NPP), which represents the amount of carbon fixed by vegetation after accounting for the carbon plants use through respiration, as well as soil organic carbon (SOC), which measures carbon stored in soil.In areas undergoing ecological restoration, NPP initially increased substantially. The study's overall results found that afforestation increased NPP by 34% during the initial restoration phase, but NPP subsequently declined by 10%. Soil organic carbon also increased, although its rate of accumulation gradually slowed over time. The researchers found that the pattern was particularly pronounced in planted forests. Over approximately three decades, planted-forest expansion accounted for an increase of around 35,000 square kilometres in the basin.More than 80% saw NPP decline within 15 yearsThe researchers then examined how long the initial increase in productivity lasted in areas where planted forests had expanded. Their analysis found that annual NPP shifted from an increasing trend to a declining trend within 15 years after planting in more than 80% of those areas. In nearly half, the decline began within 10 years.The timing is significant because the 2 main tree species highlighted by the study, Robinia pseudoacacia and Pinus tabuliformis, typically take around 50 years to reach maturity. The researchers therefore describe the decline in carbon-sequestration capacity as occurring much earlier than expected based on the trees' biological maturity. The finding does not mean that every plantation stops absorbing carbon after 10 or 15 years. Rather, it describes a shift in the trend in annual NPP across the studied planted-forest areas, from increasing to declining. The authors interpret this as evidence that carbon-sequestration saturation can occur prematurely in the basin's dryland plantations.Water availability is a major constraintThe study examined several environmental factors that could influence carbon sequestration, including soil moisture, soil texture, temperature, drought and potential evapotranspiration. Of the individual factors assessed, soil moisture was identified as the strongest individual factor controlling carbon-sequestration dynamics. The researchers also found that interactions between environmental factors could have stronger effects than individual variables alone.The climate analysis showed that maximum daily temperatures have increased across much of the basin. The researchers also found an upward trend in maximum consecutive drought days in the middle and upper reaches. In recent years, drought periods in some areas extended to as many as 180 days, compared with historical averages of about 100 days. These conditions matter because trees planted in dryland environments require sufficient water to maintain growth. The authors argue that increasing drought and declining soil moisture can therefore restrict the ability of planted forests to continue increasing their productivity.More trees may not automatically mean more carbon storageThe researchers also examined changes in land use associated with ecological restoration. They found that converting cropland to forest generally produced greater gains in soil organic carbon, with more than half of those areas showing continuous SOC accumulation. But opportunities for further cropland conversion are becoming increasingly limited, partly because of policies protecting cultivated land. By contrast, transitions from grassland to forest produced comparatively limited improvements in carbon storage. The researchers say this means the potential for further land-use changes to increase carbon sequestration is itself approaching environmental and policy limits.The findings do not argue against ecological restoration altogether. Instead, the researchers say future restoration in dryland regions needs to account more carefully for local water availability and environmental conditions. They recommend more strategic spatial planning, the use of native or locally adapted vegetation where appropriate, continued ecological monitoring and greater consideration of grassland restoration in severely water-limited areas. For the Yellow River Basin, the study suggests that increasing planted-forest area alone cannot guarantee steadily rising carbon sequestration. The long-term effectiveness of restoration will depend partly on whether newly planted vegetation can be sustained within the water and environmental limits of the landscape.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: India sees rise in both overweight and underweight
articles.summary: India News: The latest NFHS-6 survey reveals a concerning trend in India, where both obesity and underweight conditions are simultaneously increasing, challenging health policies across the nation.
articles.body: Sedentary lifestyles are often blamed for rising obesity. It is perhaps the most obvious explanation, repeated ad nauseam in this digital age, where often the entire world stays within our six-inch screen. But data from the government's latest pan-India health survey (NFHS-6) suggest something quieter, and potentially more complicated for policymakers. Below-normal BMI has stopped retreating in India even as overweight and obesity rise.The National Family Health Survey (NFHS) is the government's main source of data on health and nutrition, run by the International Institute for Population Sciences for the Union health ministry. Its sixth round, NFHS-6, covered about 6.79 lakh households across 715 districts, with fieldwork running from May 2023 to December 2024. It reports 101 indicators for India and every state and union territory except Manipur.Among women aged 15-49, the share with below-normal BMI rose marginally from 18.7% in NFHS-5 to 19.7% in NFHS-6, while the share classified as overweight or obese rose steeply from 24% to 30.7%. Hence the calculated share of women in the normal-BMI range fell from 57.3% to 49.6%, a decline of 7.7 percentage points.Men aged 15-49 are moving in the same direction. Below-normal BMI rose from 16.2% to 19.7%, while overweight or obesity increased from 22.9% to 27.3%. Hence the share of men in the normal-BMI range shrank from 60.9% to 53%, a decline of 7.9 percentage points.BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. For these indicators, NFHS classifies BMI below 18.5 as below normal and BMI of 25 or above as overweight or obese. It does not publish the normal range in between; TOI calculated that middle by subtracting the two published shares from 100.The NFHS-6 fact sheets are provisional, and without unit-level data it has not been tested whether the changes are statistically significant.Trend reversal in low BMIComparable figures for both sexes begin with NFHS-3, and below-normal BMI fell in each round until now. Among women it went from 35.6% in NFHS-3 (2005-06) to 22.9% in NFHS-4 (2015-16) and 18.7% in NFHS-5; among men, from 34.2% to 20.2% and then 16.2%.NFHS-6 is the first of these rounds in which the below-normal share rises for both sexes, and men's share, lower than women's in each earlier round, now matches it at 19.7%. Overweight has risen in every round, from 12.6% to 30.7% among women since NFHS-3 and from 9.3% to 27.3% among men.How states faredBelow-normal BMI increased from NFHS-5 in 20 of the 35 state/UT comparisons among women and 27 of 35 among men. Overweight or obesity rose even more widely, in 33 of 35 among women and 28 of 35 among men. Both rose together in 19 of the comparisons for women and 20 for men.Among women, just seven of the 35 states and Union territories in the NFHS-6 release had a calculated normal-BMI share below 50% in NFHS-5; in NFHS-6, that number has risen to 16. So in 16 states, more than half of women in the 15-49 age group are either overweight or underweight. Among men, only one of the 35 — Puducherry — was below 50% in NFHS-5. In NFHS-6, 11 are below 50%.Rajasthan recorded the sharpest increase in below-normal BMI for both sexes: from 19.6% to 27.3% among women, a rise of 7.7 percentage points, and from 14% to 24.7% among men, up 10.7 points. Other large increases in low BMI among women were in Jammu & Kashmir, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand; among men, the sharpest increases were in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Tripura and Delhi.At the other end, Lakshadweep saw the largest increase in overweight or obesity among women, from 33.5% to 50.1%, followed by Sikkim, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. Among men, the biggest increase was in Chandigarh, from 34.4% to 48.5%, followed by Goa, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat and West Bengal.The state numbers show this is not confined to a few pockets.Urban-rural divideAmong urban women, 13.2% have below-normal BMI and 42.8% are overweight or obese. Among rural women, below-normal BMI is much higher at 22.5%, while overweight or obesity stands at 25.5%. Against NFHS-5, below-normal BMI among rural women has risen from 21.2%, while the urban estimate is unchanged at 13.2%. Overweight or obesity rose in both, from 33.2% to 42.8% in urban areas and from 19.7% to 25.5% in rural areas.Men show a similar urban-rural divide. Among urban men, 14.9% have below-normal BMI and 36.3% are overweight or obese. Among rural men, 21.9% have below-normal BMI and 23% are overweight or obese. Compared with NFHS-5, low BMI among urban men rose from 13% to 14.9%, while among rural men it rose more sharply, from 17.8% to 21.9%. Overweight or obesity increased from 29.8% to 36.3% in urban areas and from 19.3% to 23% in rural areas. Among men, the rise in low BMI was larger in rural India, while the increase in excess weight was sharper in urban India.Dr Sadajit Banerjee, a Kolkata-based internal medicine and geriatrics specialist, says that as an urban doctor he has been seeing mostly a shift towards overweight. Patients increasingly arrive asking about semaglutide and tirzepatide, having read about them; those whose BMI is still within acceptable limits are advised on lifestyle change instead.Most urban Indians, he says, do not seem motivated enough to exercise or change how they live, while others are frightened of the side effects of those drugs. The patients who take up either route readily are usually the ones who already have diabetes or another metabolic disorder. At population level, the coexistence of low BMI and overweight or obesity is consistent with what the World Health Organization calls the double burden of malnutrition. Low BMI is one marker of undernutrition rather than a complete measure of it.India not following global pattern?Most of the world has been moving in one direction. A 2024 Lancet analysis by the NCD Risk Factor Collaboration, covering 200 countries and territories, found obesity rising almost everywhere between 1990 and 2022 and more than a billion people living with obesity, while adult underweight fell in most countries.That is what makes the NFHS-6 reading unusual: India's overweight share is rising in line with the global pattern, but its below-normal share is not falling. A Global Burden of Disease study put India second only to China, at 180 million adults aged 25 and older with overweight or obesity in 2021. That is a modelled estimate on a different age base.The district-level analysisThe fact sheets report these BMI measures only for women, so the district picture is a picture of women. The female BMI indicators exclude women who were pregnant or had given birth in the preceding two months.Of the 713 district records in the release, 680 can be compared with NFHS-5, where both BMI figures are available for both rounds. In 372 of those 680, or 54.7%, both ends grew at once: more women with below-normal BMI, and more women overweight or obese. All districts in Punjab, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Delhi and Goa fall below 50% on the calculated female normal-BMI measure. So do the overwhelming majority in Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Haryana and Karnataka.A normal BMI can hide muscle loss and excess fatBMI can also conceal what it is measuring. With the elderly population growing, Banerjee says he is seeing patients whose BMI is skewed by sarcopenia — too little protein and too little exercise producing muscle loss on one side and fat gain on the other. The number on the chart often stays in the normal range. Such patients may have low muscle mass and excess body fat despite an apparently normal BMI, risks that BMI alone can miss.Blood sugar also climbedNFHS-6 also tested blood sugar, on a different age base of 15 and above, against 15-49 for BMI. The share of women with high or very high blood sugar, above 140 mg/dl, or taking medication for diabetes rose from 13.5% to 17.8%; among men, from 15.6% to 20.9%. Urban prevalence is higher on both counts, at 21.9% among women and 23.9% among men, against 16.2% and 19.7% in rural areas. The fact sheets do not establish cause and effect.Overweight and obesity are rising fast, and low BMI has stopped retreating. Across much of the country both are now visible at the same time, which leaves public-health programmes carrying two problems rather than watching one give way to the other. For Banerjee, they are not two problems at all. "Overnourished or undernourished, both fall in the malnourished category," he says. Much of the chatter is about improving urban lifestyles. How rural India gets proper nutrition is the question policymakers will have to answer.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Quote of the day by MacKenzie Scott: “The leadership of people directly experiencing inequities is essential, both because…”
articles.summary: Tech News News: Some of the people best placed to describe a problem are not always the people invited to design its solution. That gap appears in many areas of publi.
articles.body: Some of the people best placed to describe a problem are not always the people invited to design its solution. That gap appears in many areas of public life, from education and healthcare to housing and economic opportunity. MacKenzie Scott has built much of her philanthropic approach around a related question: what happens when the people living with a problem are given more say in deciding how it should be addressed? In a 2022 essay, Scott wrote about the importance of supporting leaders with direct experience of inequity. Her observation was not simply about representation. It was also about knowledge, responsibility and where power sits when decisions are made on behalf of a community.Quote of the day by MacKenzie Scott“The leadership of people directly experiencing inequities is essential, both because it is informed by insights no one else can contribute, and because it seeds power and opportunity within the community itself.”Scott included the line in her March 2022 essay Helping Any of Us Can Help Us All. She was discussing her approach to giving and the importance of hearing from people whose lives are directly affected by the issues that organisations are trying to address.What is the meaning behind today’s quote by MacKenzie ScottThe wording makes two separate points. The first is about knowledge. Someone who has lived through a particular barrier may notice things that are invisible from outside it. The second is about power. When people from the affected community take leadership roles, resources and decision-making ability can remain within that community rather than being controlled entirely by outside institutions.What MacKenzie Scott means by leadership from lived experienceScott is not arguing that personal experience is the only qualification for leadership. Her wider writing points instead towards a broader principle: people who understand an issue through their own lives should have meaningful influence over the response to it.A charity working with people facing poverty, for example, may understand statistics about income, housing or employment. Someone who has personally moved between temporary accommodation and insecure work brings a different kind of information. They may know where a system becomes difficult to navigate, which requirements create unnecessary barriers, or why an apparently useful service is rarely used.Neither form of knowledge automatically replaces the other. Scott's argument is that one should not be treated as sufficient while the other is ignored.When support means giving others the power to leadThe phrase “seeds power and opportunity” takes the argument beyond consultation.There is a difference between asking people for their views and giving them the authority to act on those views. A community can be invited to a meeting, asked to complete a survey or consulted during the design of a programme without having much influence over what happens afterwards. Leadership is different because it changes who is making decisions.That is particularly relevant to philanthropy, where large institutions or wealthy donors can have substantial control over which problems receive money and which approaches are considered worth supporting. Scott has repeatedly written about moving some of that control towards the organisations receiving funding.In a 2021 essay titled 'Seeding by Ceding', she argued that people dealing directly with inequities deserved greater attention in stories about the change they were creating. She also wrote that solutions were best designed and implemented by others rather than centred on the donors providing the money.What the quote says about decision-makingThere is a practical question hidden inside Scott's words: who gets to decide what a community needs? It is easy for outside institutions to define a problem from a distance. A funding body might describe a community through poverty rates, health statistics, educational outcomes or other measurements. Those numbers can be useful, but they cannot capture every detail of how people experience a system.A person who has lived with the problem can bring another layer of information. That does not make lived experience automatically correct. Personal experience can be partial, just as institutional data can be incomplete. The point is about the value of having both perspectives in the room, particularly when decisions affect the people whose lives are being discussed.Scott's approach places particular weight on the second perspective because it is often the one with less access to money and institutional authority.How to turn the quote into everyday actionListen before deciding: Ask people affected by a decision what they actually need.Give people a real say: Listening has more value when their views can influence what happens next.Share responsibility: When working with others, let them take ownership instead of making every decision yourself.Trust people with experience: People who deal with a problem directly may understand practical solutions better than outsiders.Move beyond asking for opinions: If you ask someone for input, consider giving them a role in shaping the outcome.Make space for others to lead: Leadership does not always have to come from the person with the most authority.Share control where possible: In family, work or community decisions, involve the people who will be directly affected.Measure success together: Ask those involved whether a decision or solution actually worked, rather than judging it alone.Turn listening into action: The lesson is not simply to hear people, but to let what you hear influence your decisions.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: In 2023, a charity shelter found gold Nike Air Jordans in a donation bin; the one-of-four-or-five pair sold for $50,800
articles.summary: US News: A pair of bright gold Nike Air Jordan 3s was sitting near the bottom of a clothing donation bin at the Portland Rescue Mission in Oregon when James Fr.
articles.body: A pair of bright gold Nike Air Jordan 3s was sitting near the bottom of a clothing donation bin at the Portland Rescue Mission in Oregon when James Free, who was a participant in the shelter's transitional program, spotted them in April 2023. He set them aside for staff to inspect, and they turned out to be custom sneakers that were made for filmmaker Spike Lee and his inner circle, one of only four or five pairs produced. In December, Sotheby's sold the pair for $50,800, with the hammer price going to the Portland Rescue Mission.The shoes looked like ordinary donations at firstThe Portland Rescue Mission receives large quantities of donated clothing and shoes, which are sorted and distributed to people who need them. When Free came across the gold Jordans, their condition stood out, as they were brand new while many of the surrounding donations were used clothing and footwear.The shoes were a custom version of the Air Jordan 3 that was designed for Lee. Sotheby's described the pair as having metallic gold leather, black, white and icy-blue details, a red interior, and custom logos that were connected to Lee's production company, 40 Acres and a Mule Filmworks.The model first became publicly recognizable when Lee wore a pair at the 2019 Academy Awards. He was wearing the gold Jordans when he accepted the Oscar for adapted screenplay for BlacKkKlansman. The shoes found in Portland were not Lee's personal pair, as Sotheby's identified them as one of a small number of pairs made for Lee to give to people in his circle. The model was never released to the general public.Staff initially thought the shoes might be fakePortland Rescue Mission staff first had to determine whether the shoes were genuine. Erin Holcomb, the charity's director of staff ministry, said that the shoes initially appeared too unusual to be authentic. Staff searched for information about the model and eventually took the pair to a local sneaker business for examination, and found that the shoes were identified as genuine. Nike designer Tinker Hatfield, whose name appears on the shoes alongside Lee's, was then contacted. Hatfield authenticated the sneakers and became involved in preparing the auction lot.Nobody at the charity knew who had placed the shoes in the donation chute or why, which left the organization with a rare collector item that had arrived in exactly the same way as thousands of ordinary shoes and clothes.Hatfield also supplied material connected to the original design, and provided a replacement shoe box and signed additional material for the auction. Sotheby's included that material with the shoes, along with provenance from the Portland Rescue Mission.The estimate was nowhere near the final priceSotheby's initially estimated the pair at $15,000 to $20,000, and the auction closed on December 18, 2023, and the winning price reached $50,800. The final figure was more than twice the top end of the estimate, and the entire hammer price was designated for the Portland Rescue Mission. Sotheby's waived its seller's fee for the charity, although the auction house retained the buyer's and overhead premiums.The Guardian reported that the shoes were one of only four to five pairs custom-made for Lee and his inner circle, and also confirmed that the pair had been found in the Portland shelter's donation chute in April before being auctioned at Sotheby's in December. The donor's identity was still unknown after the sale, while the $50,800 hammer price went back to the organization that had received the anonymous donation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2021, a sealed Super Mario Bros. cartridge bought in 1986 sold for $660,000; months later, a different sealed copy reached $2 million in a private Rally sale
articles.summary: US News: A copy of Super Mario Bros. was bought as a Christmas present in late 1986 and spent 35 years at the bottom of an office desk drawer before its owner .
articles.body: A copy of Super Mario Bros. was bought as a Christmas present in late 1986 and spent 35 years at the bottom of an office desk drawer before its owner finally sold it for $660,000 in April 2021. The sealed Nintendo Entertainment System game became the most expensive video game ever sold at auction at the time, and a few months later, a different sealed copy of Super Mario Bros. changed hands privately for $2 million, which pushed the value of unopened Nintendo games into a different category altogether. Heritage Auctions recorded the $660,000 auction sale, while the later $2 million transaction was handled through Rally rather than a conventional auction.The game that stayed inside a desk drawerThe $660,000 cartridge had been purchased in late 1986 as a Christmas gift. The buyer never opened it and put it away in a desk drawer, where it remained untouched for about 35 years. The owner eventually decided to sell, with the cartridge still factory sealed. Heritage graded the game WATA 9.6 A+ and identified it as a Super Mario Bros. copy from a short production period, which had the perforated cardboard hangtab packaging and a particular code configuration that placed it within a limited production run.Heritage said that this particular version was produced in late 1986 and was among the early copies to use plastic shrink wrap rather than the earlier sticker-sealed packaging. Nintendo had moved to another packaging variation by early 1987. The cartridge was unopened after decades in storage, and its packaging corresponded to a relatively short production window. Heritage described it as the oldest factory-sealed Super Mario Bros. copy it had offered at that point.The auction record lasted only a few monthsHeritage sold the cartridge on April 4, 2021, for $660,000, and the amount included the buyer's premium and more than quadrupled the previous record for a Super Mario Bros. game, which Heritage had set at $114,000 in July 2020. In July, a sealed copy of The Legend of Zelda sold for $870,000 at Heritage, followed two days later by a sealed Super Mario 64 that reached $1.56 million. That Mario 64 sale became the first public video-game auction to cross the $1 million mark.The games were no longer being valued simply as old entertainment software, since condition, packaging variations, grading and provenance had become central to the collector market. The owner of the $660,000 Super Mario Bros. had bought it as a Christmas gift that disappeared into a desk drawer and remained there for decades. Its eventual value was determined only after collectors began paying large sums for professionally graded, unopened games.Another Mario cartridge reached $2 millionThe $2 million figure that is often associated with the 2021 Super Mario Bros. record belonged to a different copy. Rally is a platform that allowed investors to buy fractional interests in collectibles, and it acquired its sealed Super Mario Bros. cartridge for $140,000 in 2020. The company then offered shares in the game to investors, and in August 2021, those investors approved a $2 million buyout from an anonymous collector.Artnet reported that Rally had sold 3,000 shares in the game for $50 each, and the eventual $2 million transaction therefore represented a major increase over the $140,000 that Rally had paid to acquire it. However, this was not an auction unlike the $660,000 Heritage transaction, which matters because the two sales are often blended together when the 2021 video-game market is discussed. The $660,000 cartridge was bought in 1986 and sold at auction, and the $2 million cartridge was sold through Rally's fractional-ownership model.The $2 million mark eventually remained the benchmark for a Super Mario Bros. sale until 2026, when Heritage sold a different sealed copy for $3 million. That later cartridge was the highest-graded copy of an early sealed edition and became the new record for the game.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Brazil election: Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro hold one-point leads in separate runoff polls
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Two Brazilian presidential polls released on Monday produced opposite one-point leads in a possible runoff, with neither President Luiz Inacio Lula da.
articles.body: Two Brazilian presidential polls released on Monday produced opposite one-point leads in a possible runoff, with neither President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva nor Senator Flavio Bolsonaro ahead outside the surveys' margins of error.A Quaest poll put Bolsonaro at 42% and Lula at 41%, while BTG Pactual/Nexus had Lula at 46% against Bolsonaro's 45%. Both surveys had margins of error of two percentage points.Quaest gap narrows from AugustLula led Bolsonaro 44% to 39% in an August 5 Quaest poll. Bolsonaro moved ahead 42% to 40% in the September 14 survey before the difference narrowed to 42%-41% on Monday.The latest Quaest poll surveyed 2,004 people from September 17 to 20. In the first round, it put Lula at 37% and Bolsonaro at 33%, while BTG Pactual/Nexus had them at 40% and 37%, respectively. The latter survey interviewed 2,006 people from September 18 to 20.Brazil votes on October 4. If no candidate receives more than 50% of valid votes, the two leading candidates will advance to an October 25 runoff.Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term. Flavio Bolsonaro is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is barred from public office until 2030. The former president was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison in September 2025 after Brazil's Supreme Court convicted him of plotting a coup to remain in power following his 2022 election defeat.US tariffs enter campaign debateLula announced his fourth-term bid at a Workers' Party convention in Sao Paulo on August 2, putting Brazilian sovereignty at the centre of his campaign message. Two weeks later, he held a campaign launch at the May 1 stadium in Sao Bernardo do Campo, a venue associated with his early labour activism.The sovereignty theme has also featured in Brazil's trade dispute with Washington. The US imposed 25% tariffs on some Brazilian goods in July, citing alleged unfair trade practices. A separate 12.5% tariff measure affecting Brazil and several other countries was linked to US concerns over enforcement against goods produced with forced labour. Brazilian officials rejected the measures as unjustified.Lula has argued that Brazil should determine its future without foreign interference. On Monday, he said his government would hold off on using its reciprocity law against the US while negotiations continued, but could take reciprocal action if the talks failed.Lula in New York ahead of voteLula is in New York for the United Nations General Assembly. He met New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday and said their discussion included shared economic pressures, particularly household living costs.Brazil traditionally speaks first among member states at the UN General Assembly's general debate, followed by the United States as host country. Lula's New York visit comes less than two weeks before Brazil's October 4 first-round vote.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Las Vegas has a hidden world beneath its streets where hundreds of people live inside 600 miles of flood tunnels
articles.summary: US News: Las Vegas is known for its bright casinos, busy streets and round-the-clock entertainment, but beneath the city lies a very different world. Hundreds .
articles.body: Las Vegas is known for its bright casinos, busy streets and round-the-clock entertainment, but beneath the city lies a very different world. Hundreds of people have made homes inside a vast network of flood-control tunnels built to move water during heavy rainfall. The tunnels stretch for about 600 miles beneath the valley, including areas close to major resorts. For people without stable housing, these dark concrete passages have become places to sleep, cook and build small communities, even though the same tunnels can quickly become life-threatening when heavy rain arrives.How hundreds of people came to live in Las Vegas flood tunnelsThe underground network was never designed as housing. Deseret News reported that Las Vegas was built in a desert where sudden downpours can cause flash floods, leading to the construction of hundreds of miles of tunnels to collect and redirect water. Some passages are only four or five feet high, while others are large enough for people to stand comfortably. They run through parts of the city near well-known resorts, including Caesars Palace, the Rio, the Flamingo and the Orleans.The scale of the system helps explain how such a hidden community could develop. The tunnels are spread across the valley, with some sections running close to the surface and others extending much deeper underground.Daily life of this underground community in VegasFor people who have stayed there for years, the tunnels can become more than a place to sleep. VoiceofAmerica(VOA) reported on one tunnel near the Las Vegas Strip where around 30 homeless people were living. Deeper inside, there was carpet, electricity and artwork on the walls. Residents cooked meals, did laundry and followed their own rules, including keeping the area clean and respecting other people.According to Deseret News, residents had collected discarded furniture and other belongings from above ground. Some had beds, tables, chairs, coolers, bicycles and barbecue grills. In several places, furniture was raised above the ground because floodwater could rush through the tunnels without warning.The communities can also develop their own informal leadership. VOA reported one resident named Craig, known as the mayor, who had lived in his tunnel for 7 years. He earned money by selling lost golf balls collected from a nearby course and said residents took pride in not stealing from one another.Why do people stay despite the dangersLife underground is extremely difficult, but the tunnels can offer something that the streets do not. There is shelter from the desert environment, privacy and a place where people can keep their belongings. Deseret News reported about residents who had spent a decade or more underground, while others moved between different tunnels or stayed only temporarily.For some residents, the underground community can also feel familiar. VOA reported about a woman who described the people around her as a family, while also recognising that becoming comfortable there could make it harder to leave. Another resident described the tunnel simply as free rent, with running water being one of the main things missing.But the risks are constant. Floodwater is the greatest danger. Deseret News reported that residents have seen people swept away, with water and debris moving through the passages at dangerous speed. Someone deep inside a tunnel may not hear the rain above until the water is already approaching.Volunteers and non-profits try to help people leave and begin a new lifeOne of the people most closely connected to the underground community is Paul Vautrinot, who once lived there himself. According to Deseret News, Vautrinot spent 3 years in the tunnels before getting sober, entering drug court and finding regular work. He later became executive director of ShineALight, a non-profit outreach organisation that helps people living underground.His approach is based on returning to the people instead of simply asking them to come outside. He brings basic supplies such as food, water, batteries, clean socks and torches. ShineALight also helps people with housing, drug counselling and job training.Another person with a close connection to the tunnel community is Robert Banghart, the outreach director at ShineALight. According to 8NewsNow, Robert claims that there are about 600 miles of tunnels in Las Vegas and 1,500 people living in them. Every Saturday, he and about 60 to 80 volunteers, in groups of 6-8, go in the tunnels to provide peanut butter, jelly sandwiches, bottled water, first-aid kits and other items of survival. Robert knows firsthand about the life of these tunnel people as he once lived like them. As per 8NewsNow, Banghart credits Vautrinot for his recovery.VOA reported that Vautrinot regularly returned to the tunnels to persuade residents to consider rehabilitation. The organisation offered free rehabilitation to people who were ready to tackle their drug addiction, although many residents were not yet prepared to leave the underground life.What makes escaping tunnel life so difficultLeaving can mean giving up the only environment some residents have known for years. Vautrinot understood this personally because he had once built his own life underground. Deseret News reported about how he initially settled into a tunnel community, following its rules and gradually moving deeper inside as he became more established there.According to 8NewsNow, volunteer visits are an important first step because they allow outreach workers to build relationships with people who may not immediately trust outside help. The people living there are not part of a mysterious underground legend. They are trying to survive in a place never intended to become a home.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
