articles.title: In 2013, a venture-capital couple bought California land for $13.625 million, demolished the old house, built a 12,300-square-foot estate, then sold it for $56 million
articles.summary: US News: Discover how venture-capital investors Bandel and Paula Carano transformed 12 acres in Portola Valley into the stunning Villa del Prato, selling it for a record $56 million after groundbreaking design and construction.
articles.body: In 2013, venture-capital investor Bandel Carano and his wife, Paula, bought nearly 12 acres in Portola Valley, California, for $13.625 million and later developed the property into Villa del Prato, a newly built Italian-style estate. Completed in 2021, the property includes a 12,300-square-foot main residence alongside separate entertainment and pool buildings.According to The Wall Street Journal, the estate was initially listed for $85 million in February 2025 before its asking price was reduced to $65 million. It eventually sold for $56 million on November 14, 2025, setting a record for the most expensive residential sale in Portola Valley at the time.From Shorenstein property to a new estateThe Caranos bought the land from the descendants of Walter Shorenstein, the San Francisco real-estate tycoon. The land offered something increasingly rare on the Peninsula: a large, relatively flat parcel big enough for a private compound. The estate encompasses a total of 12 acres, split up into three lots. Instead of using the old home, the new construction consisted of an estate built specifically for the project. This project was completed in approximately 2021, resulting in the creation of a main home measuring 12,300 square feet. Architecturally, it used a lot of inspiration from Italian Palladian architecture, and the estate was named "Villa del Prato," which translates to a "Country House of Meadows."The house was designed by architect Andrew Skurman, with interiors by Suzanne Tucker. It has arches, loggias, stone columns, and high ceilings to create the look of an Italian countryside villa, while the land on which it sits gives it the feel of a private compound in Silicon Valley. This combination of land and location is especially valuable in the San Francisco Bay Area, where land scarcity strongly shapes real-estate prices. A study published in the Journal of Urban Economics examined how location, topography, access to employment and land-use rules affect land prices in the region, helping explain why large Peninsula parcels can command high values.Inside the 12,300-square-foot villaVilla del Prato was meant to be not just a large building but an estate consisting of multiple buildings. The estate includes three buildings: a 12,000-square-foot main house, a 6,500-square-foot entertainment building and a 2,000-square-foot pool house. The residence comprises six bedrooms and 12 bathrooms, according to the listing of the property, with interior architecture reflecting Italian design style. One distinctive feature is a 900-square-foot dressing area that can also serve as a safe room. Another feature is a 3,500-bottle wine cellar, while the entertainment building includes a ballroom and a loggia for private events and business gatherings. The exterior is also important. Its flat 12-acre site is unusual in a neighbourhood where large parcels are hard to find.From $85 million listing to $56 million saleThe Wall Street Journal also reported that when Villa del Prato was listed in February 2025, the asking price was $85 million before it was cut to $65 million and eventually sold for $56 million in November. Its buyer is said to be a resident of San Jose who had been looking for such a property for years. The sale price was far above the Caranos’ 2013 purchase price, though the difference also reflects years of development and construction.The deal was also above the previous record of $35 million for any single-family residence in Portola Valley, which was held by the 13-acre estate of Sun Microsystems founder Scott McNealy back in 2024. Villa del Prato was an estate turned into an entirely new Italian-style compound by the Caranos, who bought the land in 2013.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar remanded to 6-day ED custody amid KPSC recruitment exam row
articles.summary: BENGALURU: A special court in Bengaluru on Monday remanded suspended IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar to six days of Enforcement Directorate (ED) c.
articles.body: BENGALURU: A special court in Bengaluru on Monday remanded suspended IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar to six days of Enforcement Directorate (ED) custody in a money laundering case linked to alleged irregularities in Karnataka Public Service Commission (KPSC) recruitment.The 21st additional city civil and sessions judge and special judge for CBI and PMLA cases, Manjunath Sangreshi, remanded Gangwar to ED custody till September 26.Gangwar was produced before the court from Parappana Agrahara Central Prison, where he was in judicial custody.The ED, through special public prosecutor Maheshwari DM, had sought 14 days of custody in connection with the alleged leakage of the veterinary officer recruitment examination question paper.The agency alleged that Gangwar and Tumkur University syndicate member Basavaraj Kannale conspired to leak the question paper and collect bribes from candidates.According to the ED, Kannale allegedly collected Rs 1.50 crore from candidates, of which Rs 1.30 crore was allegedly handed over to Gangwar in cash. The agency further alleged that Rs 23 lakh was spent on purchasing gold jewellery.The ED alleged that Gangwar handed over the question paper along with answers on an HP pen drive on January 7, two days before the January 9 examination.The agency told the court that custodial interrogation of Gangwar was required to trace the alleged proceeds of crime and ascertain further details of the money laundering case.On the KPSC scam, Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar on Tuesday said the state government is legally exploring the possibility of shutting down the KPSC following widespread irregularities, while also questioning the high court’s prerogative to hand-pick specific officers to head a Special Investigation Team (SIT).Taking a hard stance on the deep-rooted corruption allegations within the recruitment body, the chief minister said the government is considering drastic measures, including shutting down the KPSC altogether, to protect candidates' futures."We are also very serious. I actually want to tell you that I am speaking about this from a legal perspective. KPSC itself has to be closed, because this is a very big issue. The chairman and others are involved, and we have received a lot of information. A lot of data is with our police. Everything has been investigated, including how it happened, who appointed whom and what was done. articles.title: An Elvis superfan paid $150,000 for a Memphis home inspired by Graceland, which its previous owners bought for $55,000; she now plans to turn its backyard caravans into another source of income
articles.summary: News News: When Elvis Presley superfan Claire Starring heard that musicians Dale Watson and Celine Lee were selling their Graceland-inspired home in Memphis, Ten.
articles.body: When Elvis Presley superfan Claire Starring heard that musicians Dale Watson and Celine Lee were selling their Graceland-inspired home in Memphis, Tennessee, she did not take long to decide. Starring was visiting the real Graceland at the time, a place she visits often.Within hours, she went to see the house and decided she wanted it. The three-bedroom, 1.5-bathroom property, known as 'Lil’ Graceland, was listed for $175,000. According to property records cited by website Realtor, Starring eventually bought it for $150,000.“I have to have this place. I don’t care how I do it, I have to have this place,” was Starring's first thought, she recalled, as quoted by Realtor. The green shag carpet inside the house was one of the first things that caught her attention. “The minute I stepped foot on the shag green carpet, I was like, ‘Oh, my gosh. I love it. We have to have this house.’”Starring, who lives in Woodstock, Georgia, bought the house despite her husband suggesting that she should not appear too interested if she wanted to negotiate the price. But she told him, “No, you pay asking price, because I want this place”.No plans to change the interiorsWatson and Lee had bought the property in 2017 for $55,000 from its original owners. They turned it into a home filled with Elvis memorabilia and items inspired by the 1950s.Starring is a former set designer and home renovator, but she does not plan to carry out major changes inside “Lil’ Graceland”. Instead, she plans to keep most of the existing design and furnishings.But she did make one immediate change after buying the house. The exterior, which had been brick-red, was painted bright turquoise on the day she completed the purchase. Inside, however, she plans to leave the property largely as it is.The house has a number of features linked to its retro and Elvis-inspired theme. Its rooms include wood panelling, vintage-style furniture, Elvis memorabilia and a green shag carpet. One room, described as a peacock-themed living room, takes inspiration from a similarly themed stained-glass room at the actual Graceland.The kitchen also has a retro look, although it has been fitted with new appliances. The property is already furnished, which was another reason Starring did not feel the need to make major changes.Plans for the backyard caravansStarring does have plans for two caravans located in the backyard. She plans to remodel them and “glamp them out” so they can be used to host guests.One of the caravans already has a full bathroom. The idea will add another way for the property to generate income while allowing visitors to experience the Elvis-themed location.“Lil’ Graceland” is already being used for several purposes. The property operates as a short-term rental on Airbnb and can also be booked as a film and photo set. It is also used as a recording studio.Visitors can book the location for a day or stay overnight to experience the property. Starring also plans to eventually use it for weddings, giving Elvis fans another way to use the Memphis property.Sun Studio equipment insideThe basement adds another part to the property's connection with music. It contains original equipment from Sun Studio, the recording service founded in the 1950s by Sam Phillips.Watson, one of the previous owners, acquired the equipment and still uses the recording studio at the house. He is expected to record another album there in October.The studio has also recently been used by bands including The Black Keys and Reverend Horton Heat. Starring plans to continue allowing fans and music industry professionals to use the property.She will keep some dates blocked for her family. Although she lives around five hours away in Georgia, she maintains the property with help from a local team in Memphis and remains in contact with the previous owners.Her family will also use the house for special occasions. “We’ll be going for Thanksgiving. We’re going to have a 1950s Thanksgiving at the house,” she said. “And then, we’ll be back for Elvis’ birthday.”Starring's Elvis ConnectionStarring's connection with Elvis began when she was a child growing up on the Isle of Man, an island in the Irish Sea between Ireland and Great Britain.She remembers that her parents were always working while she was growing up. Her mother would play Elvis' music for her, and the singer eventually became a major part of her childhood.“Sometimes, people don’t have something to believe in. I believe in God, and I’d never think that Elvis is a god ... but he was everything when I was growing up,” she said. “He was the person I talked to about everything. His music really helped me.”Starring said Elvis' journey from having very little to becoming a major music star also inspired her. “The way he came from nothing and never changed who he was ... That, to me, is massive,” she said.Her fandom is also part of her family life. Starring is the mother of a daughter, Presley Grace, and was recently married at Graceland. She said her husband is not as big an Elvis fan as she is, but he understands what the singer means to her.Starring explained that her daughter comes first, followed by rescue animals and then Elvis. “Elvis is massive in my life. So if you can deal with that, then we’re good to go. If not, then you can jog on,” she said. “He accepts my crazy, and he loves it.”“I didn’t buy it for me,” Starring explained. “I bought it for every Elvis fan. Every fan of music. Every fan of Memphis. You know, it’s a really special place.”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: How Russia, Ukraine traded strikes overnight on oil, energy sites as Zelenskyy visited US - videos
articles.summary: Europe News: Russia launched a massive overnight barrage of missiles and drones across Ukraine, striking oil, gas and industrial facilities and killing at least fo.
articles.body: Russia launched a massive overnight barrage of missiles and drones across Ukraine, striking oil, gas and industrial facilities and killing at least four people, Ukrainian officials told Tuesday.The attack targeted a key oil and gas facility in Ukraine’s Poltava region with ballistic missiles, according to Reuters.Moscow also struck industrial sites in the southeastern cities of Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad, while an attack on an energy facility in the northern Chernihiv region cut power supplies to nearly 100,000 consumers.The latest exchange of aerial attacks came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was visiting the United States.Days ago, US President Donald Trump raised concerns that both sides should stop targeting each other’s fuel infrastructure.Russia has intensified its air campaign in recent months, hitting economic targets ranging from businesses and ports to logistics hubs, even as fighting along the front line has largely stalled more than four years after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Both sides deny targeting civilians.Strikes hit Ukraine's industrial heartlandRussian forces simultaneously targeted industrial enterprises in Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Telegram.The region is a major industrial hub, home to machine-building, steel-making and other manufacturing industries.Russia used missiles, drones and artillery against four districts, killing four people and injuring six in Dnipro, Hanzha said. A business and warehouse premises were also badly damaged.Ukraine's air force said the Russian barrage included an unspecified number of Oniks anti-ship and ballistic missiles, four cruise missiles and 212 drones.Russia's defence ministry said its forces struck industrial and military facilities in Ukraine, including targets in the fuel and energy sector, as well as port infrastructure and sea vessels serving the Ukrainian military.Businesses were also damaged in Pavlohrad and Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of Zelenskyy, Hanzha said.In neighbouring Chernihiv region, a Russian strike on an energy facility disrupted electricity supplies to nearly 100,000 consumers, according to an electricity distributor.Poltava region was also hit in what governor Vitalii Diakivnych described as a "massive" attack. Russian forces struck an industrial enterprise and a critical infrastructure facility, though officials did not immediately provide further details.Russia's defence ministry said its forces had struck an oil refinery in Kremenchuk, in the Poltava region.Ukraine strikes back inside RussiaUkraine has meanwhile stepped up its own drone campaign against targets deep inside Russia, including oil refineries and major online retailers.Ukrainian drones struck civilian targets in Russia's Samara region on the Volga River, killing one person and injuring four, the local governor said. The region is home to strategically important industrial facilities, including oil refineries.Russia's defence ministry said its air defence units destroyed 297 Ukrainian drones over various Russian regions overnight.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2011, a runner left Disneyland for New York City; 75 days and 3,000 miles later, he had crossed America while running up to 50 miles a day
articles.summary: US News: In 2011, ultramarathon runner Dean Karnazes undertook a grueling challenge, running from Disneyland to New York City in 75 days. Covering 3,000 miles, he aimed to promote physical activity among families while battling extreme weather and physical demands.
articles.body: In 2011, ultramarathon runner Dean Karnazes set himself a challenge that turned the familiar idea of a cross-country road trip into a relentless endurance test. Starting at Disneyland in California on February 25, he set out to run all the way to New York City. Over the next 75 days, Karnazes covered nearly 3,000 miles, routinely running 40 to 50 miles a day through deserts, mountains, plains and cities. The journey was organised with Live! with Regis and Kelly and was intended to encourage children and families to become more physically active.A coast-to-coast run beginsAccording to CBS News, Karnazes was already known for pushing the limits of long-distance running before he began his Run Across America. His previous achievements included completing 50 marathons in 50 states over 50 consecutive days, as well as competing in some of the world's most demanding ultramarathons. The 2011 challenge, however, required him to keep moving for more than two months, making it a sustained cross-country effort rather than a single race.The idea came from a collaboration between Karnazes and the Disney ABC television network. For Karnazes, the opportunity came from his desire to see America on foot, while the television show aimed to encourage exercise among younger viewers. This particular trek became a daily segment of Live! with Regis and Kelly. The task was enormous. The route was more than 3,000 miles long and passed through 16 states and the District of Columbia. Karnazes normally ran about 40 to 50 miles a day, which meant that his daily run would be almost double the distance of a normal marathon.At that time, Karnazes was reportedly expected to run for up to 14 hours a day. It was not just a matter of putting one foot in front of the other continuously. Karnazes and his support team had to manage his nutrition, hydration and recovery while he kept running. According to Karnazes' coach Jason Koop, Karnazes needed around 8,000 calories a day, much of it consumed while running.Heat, snow and thousands of milesThe route exposed Karnazes to different conditions. He faced extreme heat while crossing the Arizona desert, along with snow and sleet in mountainous areas and intense humidity farther east. Instead of waiting for favourable weather, he had to keep moving through changing conditions as the miles added up.The physical demands of such sustained running are considerable. Research published in the Journal of Applied Physiology examined the physiological responses of ultramarathon athletes during prolonged exercise, including changes in oxygen consumption, cardiovascular function, body temperature and muscle performance. The findings help illustrate the strain placed on the body when endurance exercise is extended over many hours and repeated across consecutive days.Karnazes' account offers a vivid illustration of that continuous demand. He explained that he managed to cover more than 300 miles a week for about two and a half months while also visiting schools, giving interviews and taking part in organised 5K runs. There were no traditional days off during the 75-day adventure, so he regularly faced the physiological challenges seen in ultramarathon studies.Another component of his daily routine was food. Since he had to cover about 40 to 50 miles each day, he could not put off his meals for the latter half of the day. His team developed a way for him to eat nutritious food while running. The people he met along the way were also important. Local children and runners accompanied him for stretches of the route, and organised 5K races gave communities a chance to join in.75 days from Disneyland to New YorkCBS News also notes that Karnazes completed his journey in May 2011, about two and a half months after he set out. He arrived at the Live! with Regis and Kelly studios in New York on May 10 after running almost 3,000 miles, with an American flag on the last leg of the trip. His wife and son were there waiting to meet him. The final figures were about 3,000 miles, 75 days and an average of 40 to 50 miles a day. Over 50 pairs of running shoes had been consumed in the process, and 5K runs organised along the way had helped raise $177,865 for Action for Healthy Kids.Looking back, Karnazes said the distance did not define the experience. He said the challenge was not only physical but also environmental, with mountains, deserts and changing weather creating a very different pattern from an ordinary marathon. What began as an exercise-promotion program at Disneyland became one of Karnazes' most memorable runs. He ran for 75 straight days across the country, covering distances that would have been a tough marathon for almost anyone else.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: US couple donates $250 million to animal support and welfare organisations, allowing veterinary care access to millions of families and their pets over the next five years
articles.summary: US News: When you get a pet, they are not just another being added to your family; they become the centre of it. The one who holds all the love from all the me.
articles.body: When you get a pet, they are not just another being added to your family; they become the centre of it. The one who holds all the love from all the members and becomes the emotional cornerstone of belongingness in the house. But across America, pet care and health are not something easily accessible and financially affordable for everyone. Hoping to change this and allow millions of pet owners to access critical veterinary care beyond their budgets, a philanthropic organisation has announced a groundbreaking $250 million commitment over the next five years.Made by the Dave & Cheryl Duffield Foundation, it represents one of the largest private philanthropic investments ever made in American history to expand access to nonprofit community veterinary care. The Duffield Big Best for Pets will support community-based organisations working to expand access to veterinary care for family pets, invest in research and other strategies to advance progress in closing the gap in access to veterinary care. The initiative will roll out multiple investments and grant opportunities over the next 5 years, and the first 2 launch have launched already.Duffield Boost Grants is a collective $2.5 million grant opportunity that will provide 250 grants of $10,000 each to nonprofit community veterinary care providers nationwide. Expanding Access Grants will establish a $10 million pool for significant, multi-year grants for established nonprofit community veterinary clinics that are ready to expand their capacity to reach more pets in need.“The lack of access to affordable veterinary care is one of the most urgent and actionable challenges facing pets and the people who love them,” said Amy Mills, vice president of access to care at the Dave & Cheryl Duffield Foundation. “Through Big Bet for Pets, we are investing in a future where every pet has access to the veterinary care they need, and every family can care for the animals they love.”Success in building and delivering innovation at six enterprise software companies, including PeopleSoft, Workday, and today, Ridgeline, has allowed billionaire software engineer, Cornell alum, and philanthropist Dave Duffield to give away heaps of the proceeds to charitable causes close to his heart, and to that of his wife, Cheryl. The couple has already donated more than $300 million to companion animal support and welfare organisations.Dave and Cheryl Duffield have funded companion-animal causes for more than 30 years, most notably through Maddie's Fund, which they built into one of the largest private foundations supporting shelters and companion-animal organisations. The Dave & Cheryl Duffield Foundation itself was established in 2016 and also backs programs pairing veterans with service dogs and supporting local public service organisations, alongside Maddie's Fund and Liberty Dogs.Their latest donation takes the total past $500 million with the 'Big Bet for Pets', an initiative that builds on this legacy by addressing the veterinary care gap in America, which the foundation estimates impacts 50 million dogs and cats nationwide. This gap is largely the result of financial barriers to care, leaving millions of pets without routine, preventive, and lifesaving veterinary services.“Pets are members of our families, and they need veterinary care to live long, healthy lives,” said Dave Duffield in a statement. “For too many families, that care is not easy to find or afford. Big Bet for Pets is our way of investing in a stronger, more accessible safety net for these special animals.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2003, eight artists secretly built a 750-square-foot apartment inside a US mall and lived there for four years before security found them
articles.summary: US News: Back in 2003, eight artists embarked on an unusual creative experiment inside Providence Place, a shopping mall in Providence, Rhode Island. Led by ar.
articles.body: Back in 2003, eight artists embarked on an unusual creative experiment inside Providence Place, a shopping mall in Providence, Rhode Island. Led by artist Michael Townsend, the group secretly constructed a 750-square-foot apartment in an unused section of the shopping centre. They furnished the hidden space with everyday items, including a sofa, television and gaming console, and used it as a place to spend time together. The artists continued their secret project for approximately four years, staying there intermittently before mall security eventually discovered the apartment in 2007. What began as an experiment in reclaiming commercial space later became the subject of the documentary Secret Mall Apartment, directed by Jeremy Workman, and a community arts initiative involving the same shopping centre.How the secret mall apartment was createdThe project was organised by Michael Townsend and involved seven other artists: Adriana Valdez-Young, Colin Bliss, Andrew Oesch, Greta Scheing, James Mercer, Emily Ustach and Jay Zehngebot. The group had connections to Providence’s creative community and had experienced the loss of artists’ spaces during redevelopment in the city. Their project inside Providence Place was influenced by concerns about commercialisation, gentrification and the disappearance of independent artistic environments. Rather than simply seeking free accommodation, the artists viewed the apartment as an artistic and social experiment. They wanted to explore how people could use a commercial property in a way that differed from its intended purpose.Inside the 750-square-foot apartmentThe hidden apartment was constructed in an unused area within the mall’s structure, near the cinema and parking facilities. The artists concealed the space behind a wall made from cinderblocks and installed a lockable door. Over time, they transformed the empty area into a furnished living space. The apartment reportedly contained a sofa, television, PlayStation, books, photo albums and other household objects. The group also brought in appliances, including a waffle-maker. The space did not have running water, meaning the residents relied on public facilities in the mall. They also used the shopping centre’s electricity, making the apartment dependent on the infrastructure of the building they had entered without permission.The artists lived there intermittentlyAlthough the apartment existed from 2003 to 2007, the artists did not necessarily live inside it continuously. Members visited and stayed in the space at different times, turning it into a meeting point where they could socialise, rest and work on creative ideas. The group initially expected the project to last only about a week, but the experiment continued for several years. The apartment gradually became more elaborate as the artists added furniture and personal belongings. Their activities demonstrated how an ordinary commercial environment could be transformed into a private space, even though the arrangement was unauthorised and hidden from the mall’s management.How the secret was eventually discoveredThe apartment remained undetected for approximately four years. In 2007, Townsend invited an artist from Hong Kong to visit the space. The visitor’s presence attracted the attention of mall security, which subsequently discovered the hidden apartment. Townsend later acknowledged that bringing an outsider into the space violated one of the group’s rules. The discovery brought the experiment to an end and led to legal consequences for Townsend. While the project involved eight artists, Townsend became the principal person associated with the incident and accepted responsibility for his involvement.Michael Townsend faced a trespassing chargeFollowing the discovery, Townsend was initially charged with breaking and entering. The charge was later reduced to misdemeanour trespassing. He pleaded no contest and received six months of probation in October 2007. Providence Place also banned him from entering the shopping centre for life. The incident raised questions about property rights, artistic freedom and the limits of creative intervention in privately owned commercial spaces. For the artists, the apartment represented an attempt to challenge the conventional use of a shopping mall. For the property’s management, however, the hidden construction and unauthorised occupation created security and legal concerns.The project became a documentaryThe story later inspired Secret Mall Apartment, a documentary directed by Jeremy Workman. The film combines archival footage recorded by the artists with interviews conducted years after the apartment was discovered. The footage provides a record of the group’s construction work, daily activities and unusual living arrangement. The documentary also examines the broader social and economic issues surrounding the project, including gentrification and the displacement of artists from creative spaces. Actor Jesse Eisenberg was involved as an executive producer. The film premiered at the SXSW Film Festival in 2024 and subsequently received a theatrical release in 2025.The mall reconnected with the artistsNearly two decades after the apartment was discovered, Providence Place revisited the story through a community arts initiative. The shopping centre lifted Townsend’s lifetime ban and hosted screenings of Secret Mall Apartment. It also recreated the hidden apartment in a cinema lobby, using furniture and objects inspired by the original space. The recreation was not located in the apartment’s original position. The initiative included discussions, art installations, workshops and collaborations with local educational institutions. It represented a change in the relationship between the mall and the artists, turning a former controversy into an opportunity for public engagement and cultural programming.Providence Place turned the controversy into an arts campaignAccording to the International Council of Shopping Centers, the initiative was designed to reconnect Providence Place with the local creative community. The programme included tape-art installations, workshops and an augmented-reality project involving students from the Rhode Island School of Design. A wooden model of the mall was also created by artist Colin Bliss, one of the original participants. ICSC reported strong audience engagement and publicity results from the campaign, including increased visitor numbers during its first four Saturdays. These figures were presented as campaign results and should be understood as claims made by the organisers rather than independently audited measurements.Where are the artists now?The artists continued along different professional paths after the apartment project. Townsend remained involved in artistic work, while Valdez-Young pursued work in design research and education. Zehngebot continued his career as an artist. Other members of the group also remained connected to the arts and education sectors. Their reunion for the documentary offered an opportunity to revisit the motivations behind the apartment and reflect on how their lives had changed. The project, which began as a secret occupation of commercial space, eventually became a documented example of experimental art, urban change and the complicated relationship between artists and property owners.A secret experiment with a lasting legacyThe Secret Mall Apartment project stands out because it combined an unconventional living arrangement with questions about the future of creative spaces. The artists’ actions were unauthorised, but the project also reflected concerns about redevelopment and the loss of places where artists could work and live. Its later transformation into a documentary and public arts programme gave the story a second chapter. What began as a concealed apartment inside a shopping mall ultimately became a subject of public discussion, bringing together the artists, the property management and the wider Providence community.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: US Streamers News: Candace Owens is facing renewed scrutiny after a viral social media post questioned her account of a Turning Point USA (TPUSA) school event in Idaho. .
articles.body: Candace Owens is facing renewed scrutiny after a viral social media post questioned her account of a Turning Point USA (TPUSA) school event in Idaho. The post, shared by Cinema Shogun, accused the conservative commentator of reading a potentially fake parent email on her podcast. The dispute has now raised fresh questions about the assembly, school security and the claims being made about students' experience.Candace Owens' TPUSA school assembly claims spark fresh questionsThe controversy centres on a September 17 event at Nampa Christian School, where Erika Kirk addressed more than 500 students during a Club America gathering. Owens questioned whether students had freely chosen to attend, citing messages and complaints she said came from parents.TPUSA spokesperson Andrew Kolvet disputed her account, saying attendance was optional and that three students chose to opt out. The disagreement has since expanded beyond attendance, with attention turning to Owens' use of a parent's alleged email about locked doors during the assembly.Cinema Shogun's post challenged the email's credibility, arguing that the school routinely keeps its doors locked during school hours. Nampa Christian Schools confirms on its website that its buildings remain locked during the school day, except for the main entrance, where visitors must register. That policy, however, does not by itself establish what happened inside the school during the event.Viral Candace Owens clip questions locked doors and student safetyThe clip shared alongside the online criticism takes a different approach, focusing on whether the school's security procedures were being presented without context. The speaker questions the implications of locked doors during a school assembly and raises concerns about parental notice and student participation.The full remarks, as provided in the clip, read:"This person however goes on and says, but the doors were indeed locked. And as a parent, that raises questions for me. If bringing a particular speaker or organization onto a school campus requires students to be behind locked doors during the presentation, at what point should the administration ask whether that is the appropriate environment for middle and high school students during a required school assembly? This also makes me question Turning Point USA and their care for the safety of children. Perhaps locking the doors was entirely intended as a security measure to protect my students. But if that level of security was considered necessary, I believe parents should have been informed beforehand and given a meaningful choice regarding their child's participation. I just want to know one thing. You ready? Why the fuck you lying? Why you always lying? Oh my God. Stop fucking lying. Always lying to me. You're lying so much. You're making it hard for me. Every time you tell me something, I figure that you're lying. Ooh, it's almost like you're faking. Oh yeah. Yeah, I know you're lying, but you sound excited. And you know that I know that you're lying. Oh girl."The clip's accusation adds another layer to an already heated dispute. Still, the school's general security policy does not confirm whether Owens' email was fabricated or whether students were prevented from leaving the assembly. Those questions remain central to the debate, as competing accounts continue to circulate online.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2002, a Detroit lawyer bought Berry Gordy’s 1917 Motown Mansion for $250,000, restored the 10,500-sq-ft landmark and sold it for $1.65 million in 2017
articles.summary: US News: A century-old Detroit mansion with deep ties to the city’s music and industrial history once changed hands for just $250,000 before a painstaking rest.
articles.body: A century-old Detroit mansion with deep ties to the city’s music and industrial history once changed hands for just $250,000 before a painstaking restoration helped it sell for $1.65 million. Known as the Motown Mansion, the 10,500-square-foot residence at 918 W. Boston Blvd. was built in 1916-17 for lumberman Nels Michelson and later became the home of Motown Records founder Berry Gordy Jr. Historic Detroit identifies the property as the Nels Michelson Mansion and documents its origins, architecture and notable owners. Gordy bought the house in 1967 and lived there during a pivotal period for Motown before eventually selling it to Detroit attorney Cynthia F. Reaves, who restored the landmark and later sold it in 2017.A mansion built for a Detroit lumber baronThe story of the property began long before Motown. Nels Michelson, who was born in Denmark in 1840, immigrated to the United States in 1866 and built a successful career in the lumber industry. He established the Grayling Lumber Company in 1906 and later entered the real-estate business through the Michelson Land and Home Company. Michelson commissioned architect John W. Case to design the grand residence, which was completed in 1917. The house was created in an Italian Renaissance style and featured the elaborate craftsmanship associated with Detroit’s grand early-20th-century residences.Historic Detroit notes that Michelson lived at the Boston Boulevard property until the 1920s. The mansion subsequently passed to Leonard A. Young, owner of the L. A. Young Spring & Wire Company, who expanded the estate significantly.The additions that transformed the estateYoung added a large Athletic Building to the property in 1926. The approximately 4,000-square-foot structure included an Olympic-sized swimming pool, a gymnasium, billiard room and two bowling alleys. The additions made the property more than a formal residence. It became an expansive entertainment compound, with passageways connecting different sections of the estate. The main house itself featured marble, elaborate woodwork, carved mantels, stained and beveled glass and other decorative details. The estate eventually became associated with one of Detroit’s most influential cultural figures.Berry Gordy brings Motown history to the mansionBerry Gordy Jr., the founder of Motown Records, purchased the mansion in 1967. He lived there from 1967 to 1969, during a period when Motown was producing music from artists including The Supremes, The Four Tops, Smokey Robinson and Stevie Wonder. The mansion became a setting for parties and gatherings connected with the Motown world. The Washington Post reported that Diana Ross and Aretha Franklin sang at Gordy’s parties, while Stevie Wonder played the grand piano. The Jackson 5 also had connections to the property during its Motown years.Gordy eventually moved his music operation to Los Angeles but retained ownership of the Detroit mansion for decades. The property continued to carry the Motown association long after he stopped living there.A $250,000 purchase and four-year restorationWhen Cynthia Reaves returned to Detroit from Washington, D.C., she became interested in the house. She had grown up across the street from the mansion and remembered seeing celebrities arrive for parties. The Washington Post reported that Reaves bought the property from Gordy in 2002 for $250,000. Rather than treating it simply as a real-estate investment, she undertook a major rehabilitation designed to preserve its historic character.A Michigan State Historic Preservation Office record says Reaves used state historic-preservation tax credits and spent four years rehabilitating the house. The work included restoring wood surfaces, decorative painting and plaster, updating mechanical systems, restoring the landscape and rehabilitating much of the carriage house and Athletic Building. The restoration later received a Michigan historic-preservation award. The Washington Post reported that Reaves retained as much of the mansion’s original architecture as possible while bringing the property back into use.From $250,000 to a $1.65 million saleAfter more than a decade under Reaves’ ownership, the restored mansion went on the market in 2015 for $1.295 million. The property included the 10,500-square-foot main house, the adjoining pool house and a carriage house, set across approximately 2.2 acres. It ultimately remained on the market for about two years. In August 2017, the property sold for $1.65 million, exceeding its $1.595 million asking price at the time. CBS Detroit reported that the buyer was a Detroit native returning from San Francisco. The sale was followed by an estate auction featuring furniture, antiques and memorabilia associated with Gordy and Motown. Among the items offered were Gordy’s Steinway piano, photographs, Motown records and other pieces connected to the mansion’s musical past.Today, the property remains known as the Motown Mansion, but its story extends well beyond Berry Gordy. From Michelson’s lumber fortune to Young’s expansion, Gordy’s Motown years and Reaves’ preservation work, the Boston Boulevard residence reflects several chapters of Detroit’s architectural, industrial and musical history.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: One of history's most famous sayings about Rome may be wrong, new study suggests
articles.summary: The Roman Empire's vast road network favored Constantinople as a key overland travel hub, a study says, yet experts argue Rome remained the true center of power.
articles.body: A sweeping new study of the Roman Empire's vast road network is challenging the age-old saying, "All roads lead to Rome." The study, published Sept. 15 in the journal Nature Communications, analyzed roughly 190,000 miles of Roman roads spanning Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. The team combined existing data to create a new map of the Roman Empire's road network and analyze its structure on an empire-wide scale. CONSTRUCTION WORKERS CLEARING OLD BOMBS UNEXPECTEDLY FIND 'IMPORTANT' ANCIENT SANCTUARY The study's lead researcher, Tom Brughmans, a classical archaeologist at Aarhus University in Denmark, and his colleagues found that Rome was not uniquely central to the empire's road network, with provincial capitals playing key roles in overland travel. Constantinople, now known as Istanbul, Turkey, emerged as a far more central hub for overland travel after Emperor Constantine made it the imperial capital in the fourth century A.D. Constantinople's location between Europe and Asia made it exceptionally central to travel across the empire, according to the researchers. Therefore, the phrase "all roads lead to Rome" — coined centuries after the Roman Empire fell — may not reveal the whole story. ANCIENT CLUE CRACKS OPEN A 2,000-YEAR-OLD MYSTERY NEAR FAMED COLOSSEUM Brughmans told Fox News Digital that the proverb, which he described as medieval in origin, should not be taken literally — noting that none of the roads in Roman Britain actually led to Rome. "Rome is the center of the empire. This is where power lies." "It is quite surprising how persistently this maxim has shaped popular understanding of Roman roads," he said. "It’s fair to say our study complicates the proverb," Brughmans added. "I prefer to say, ‘All roads lead to Rome and everywhere else.'" RARE PAGAN MASTERPIECE EMERGES NEAR WHERE ST PAUL SPREAD TEACHINGS OF CHRISTIANITY Taco Terpstra, a professor of history and classics at Northwestern University in Illinois, told Fox News Digital the findings don't diminish Rome's importance as the center of the empire — nor do the study's authors argue otherwise. Terpstra, who was not involved in the research, noted that Constantinople "was only created as such in the fourth century." "Before that, it was a sleepy fishing town called Byzantium," he said. "So, we have to be careful a little bit about what time period we’re looking at." He added, "But once Constantinople becomes de facto the capital of the empire, it is clear that it attracts a lot of overland connectivity." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Rome did remain the center of political, military and ideological power for centuries, Terpstra said. "Rome is the center of the empire. This is where power lies," he said, noting that the empire's second-largest city, Alexandria, dwarfed in comparison with roughly half Rome's population. "This is where the emperor is. This is where the Senate is. ... [It was the] largest city in the empire, a million inhabitants." The study also examined another hallmark of Roman engineering: the remarkable straightness of its roads, though difficult terrain often forced routes to deviate from a direct path. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The roads were "about as straight as the Romans could make them" given the technology available at the time, Terpstra said. The roads initially served a military purpose, the professor added. They allowed troops to move quickly through conquered territory before also taking on an important economic role. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "The roads in the first instance, and it’s often forgotten, were military infrastructure," he said. "These were in the first place, after the conquest, intended to move troops quickly." And although Roman roads have stood the test of time and remain a marvel of ancient engineering, Terpstra said they were secondary to maritime transportation across the empire — which was far cheaper when it came to transporting goods. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The main transportation network of the Roman Empire is maritime," he said. "That is really where the major connectivity lies."

articles.title: Developing El Niño becomes strongest on record weeks before expected peak
articles.summary: Scientists say the developing El Niño is now the strongest on record with weather impacts already being felt around the world.
articles.body:
The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring Pacific Ocean temperatures.

Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El Niño of 2015.

Some longer-term measures of El Niño have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year.

El Niño can cause major shifts in weather patterns around the world, with the Met Office saying many of the expected impacts are already being felt.

El Niño set to be 'strongest in living memory', says Met Office

What is El Niño and why could it mean record temperatures?

El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year.

Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards.

Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world.

Forecasters track the development of El Niño by watching temperatures in a key region of the Pacific Ocean. When these are consistently 0.5C above normal, an El Niño is declared.

There are different ways of measuring the strength of El Niño, however.

The records that have now been broken relate to daily measurements of sea surface temperature compared with the long term historical average.

This is called the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI).

Many scientists - including forecasters in the USA and Australia - also consider an alternative measure known as the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI).

This measures how warm the key El Niño region is relative to the rest of the tropical oceans, meaning it takes into account the background warming caused by climate change.

By the RONI index the current El Niño is not yet a record-breaker - but it is likely that more announcements will follow in the coming weeks.

Professor Adam Scaife, Head of Long Range Prediction at the Met Office, said: "We have been signalling for months that the developing El Niño will be an unprecedented event.

"The fact that it has already exceeded previous records – with several weeks to go before it peaks later this year – shows the enormity of this El Niño."

Impacts of El Niño already being felt globally

Every El Niño is different, therefore impacts on global weather patterns are not guaranteed.

And the unprecedented strength of this El Niño does not necessarily mean it will have unprecedented impacts on the weather.

Professor Scaife said: "Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide."

El Niño increases the odds of storms and floods in some regions and of drought and wildfires in others.

El Niño years tend to bring below-average monsoon rainfall in India, which is already being reflected in this year's data.

Statistics from the India Meteorological Department show that, until 22 September the southwest monsoon had brought 15% less rain than normal.

Another typical impact of El Niño is reduced hurricane activity in the Atlantic due to changes in wind patterns high in the atmosphere.

So far in 2026 there have been no Atlantic hurricanes, setting a new record for the latest date without a hurricane forming since satellite monitoring of storms began.

Other possible effects - some of which are already being felt - include the increased risk of floods in coastal parts of Ecuador, Peru and the southern USA, and the enhanced threat of drought and wildfires in Brazil, Australia and Indonesia.

These weather impacts can have significant knock on effects for on crop yields, food security and economies around the globe.

The UK is thousands of miles from the tropical Pacific and so the effects of El Niño tend to be less clear-cut than in other regions.

However, it does bring the increased chance of wet and stormy conditions across north-west Europe during the late autumn and early winter.

A forecast released by the Met Office this autumn stated that there were already "signals for increased rainfall and storminess in autumn here in the UK", especially into November and December.

The winter of 2015 and 2016, which coincided with a very strong El Niño, brought a succession of major storms delivering what experts at the time described as the most extreme flooding on record.

In addition to storminess, El Niño can also be associated with UK cold spells in the late winter - but the link is not a strong one and the past evidence is mixed.

The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El Niño.

However, 2006/2007 was also an El Niño winter and that was unseasonably warm.

As this unprecedented El Niño approaches its likely peak towards the end of 2026, scientists will continue to monitor its development - and its impact on weather around the world.

articles.title: UN warns of rising Yemen displacement as thousands flee to Djibouti
articles.summary: Renewed fighting could drive 10,000 across the Red Sea and displace more than 230,000 internally, UNHCR says.
articles.body:
The number of refugees fleeing Yemen across the Red Sea to Djibouti could reach 10,000 as result of renewed fighting in the country, while internal displacement inside Yemen could swell to more than 230,000, the United Nations has warned.

The Iran-aligned Houthi rebels seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline earlier this month in a dramatic offensive that has left hundreds of people on both sides dead, threatened global trade, and pushed up energy prices.

The latest fighting between the Houthis and forces loyal to the Aden-based government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, has set off a new humanitarian crisis.

More than 100,000 civilians have been uprooted inside Yemen, while others have risked dangerous sea crossings to escape the violence.

“Intensifying fighting in Yemen could drive more mass displacement,” United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) spokesperson Babar Baloch told reporters in Geneva on Tuesday.

More than 3,000 people fled across the Red Sea to Djibouti over several days earlier this month, Djibouti state media reported. The UNHCR said it was bracing for that number to rise significantly, especially after mid-October when the current difficult sea conditions are expected to improve.

The agency and its partners are now “planning for more than 10,000 arrivals in Djibouti” in the coming months, Baloch said.

At the same time, the number of people displaced within Yemen by the recent fighting could swell from more than 130,000 today to more than 230,000, he said.

That comes on top of the more than 5.2 million people who were already internally displaced in Yemen before the fighting resumed.

Baloch warned that the renewed conflict was deepening an already dire crisis in the country, where an estimated 22 million people require humanitarian assistance.

He warned that a severe funding shortfall was hampering the response to the emergency, with the UNHCR’s Yemen operation currently just 18 percent funded for 2026.

The agency estimated that $25m is urgently needed to provide approximately 231,000 people with immediate aid.

Meanwhile, the UNHCR’s Djibouti operations are only 15 percent funded, with the agency appealing for $13.5m “to ensure arrivals can access registration, reception, protection, and other essential services”.

articles.title: Sir Sean Connery's family plans new film-making centre in Edinburgh
articles.summary: It will be named after the James Bond actor, who worked as a milkman in the Scottish capital before becoming a Hollywood star.
articles.body:
The family of Sir Sean Connery has announced plans for a new filmmaking centre in Edinburgh.

It will be named after the James Bond actor, who worked as a milkman in the Scottish capital before becoming a Hollywood star.

His children say they want it to provide training for the next generation of Scotland's film and TV talent and help them build lasting careers.

They said their father "understood that while talent may be distributed equally, opportunity is not, and that those who demonstrate determination and endeavour should have the chance to fulfill their potential".

They have unveiled plans to open the NFTS Sean Connery Institute in Edinburgh city centre within the next 18 months.

It is the product of a partnership between the Sean Connery Foundation and the National Film and Television School (NTFS).

It would be a new, permanent home for the NTFS, which would deliver training, as well screenings, masterclasses and events.

Sir Sean's children said their father was "immensely proud" of his Scottish roots and he would be pleased they were deepening their relationship with Edinburgh.

They said: "Our father believed deeply in fairness, hard work, and supporting talented people in need."

And they added: "We are proud to make this long-term commitment in his name and in keeping with the values he held dear."

NTFS director, Jon Wardle, said: "Together with the Sean Connery Foundation, we have an extraordinary opportunity to build on Sean's legacy and his deep connection to Scotland by creating a genuine pathway into and through the Scottish screen industry."

Sir Sean was born in Edinburgh 1930 went on to play Bond in six films. He also appeared in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade and The Hunt for Red October.

He won an Oscar in 1988 for his performance as Jim Malone in The Untouchables.

In October 2020 Sir Sean died peacefully in his sleep in the Bahamas, having been "unwell for some time", his son said.

The Sean Connery Foundation was set up in late 2022 with the aim of supporting emerging Scottish talent primarily in film-making and golf.

It has worked with the NTFS since 2023 on the Sean Connery Talent Lab - an intensive year-long development programme bringing together emerging Scottish writers, directors, producers, cinematographers and editors.

Sir Sean's son Jason is also the co-owner of First Stage Studio a film studio based in Edinburgh's Port of Leith.

The studio has homed multiple productions including Edinburgh set Netflix show Department Q.

articles.title: Trump open to meeting Iran’s president on UN sidelines: Rubio
articles.summary: President Trump is open to meeting the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly while he is in New York, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday. Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser, made the remarks in an interview with Fox News, saying the president operates on the “common…
articles.body:
President Trump is open to meeting the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly while he is in New York, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday.

Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser, made the remarks in an interview with Fox News, saying the president operates on the “common sense” that there’s no harm in engaging or talking to someone.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi are part of a “core” delegation to whom the State Department provided visas to attend the global summit, despite more than six months of war between the U.S. and Iran, which the U.S. and Israel launched together on Feb. 28.

“I think the president is open to a meeting with him [Pezeshkian] or anybody,” Rubio said when asked if Trump would meet with the delegation.

“Whether something productive will come out of it, it’s harder to tell because the ultimate decisionmaker in Iran is the supreme leader, and the supreme leader is a radical Shia cleric,” Rubio added.

In another interview with NBC’s “Today,” Rubio reiterated that Trump is open to a meeting with the Iranian president, but “I don’t think anything is scheduled at this point.”

“If it has the prospects of leading to something positive and ultimately achieving the goal of what this is all about, and that is the fact that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran stalled over the collapse of a joint memorandum of understanding that was meant to impose a ceasefire and open transit through the Strait of Hormuz.

Military strikes between the U.S. and Iran resumed this month after about six weeks of quiet, with Iran targeting oil ships in the strait, American bases in the region and U.S. allies. The U.S. has imposed a blockade on Iranian oil exports and struck military targets, although the U.S. was accused of hitting a wedding celebration, resulting in civilian casualties.

Meanwhile, the Houthis in Yemen, backed by Iran, have disrupted energy exports through the Red Sea, further sending gas and diesel prices soaring .

Trump is scheduled to meet with members of the Gulf Cooperation Council on Tuesday to discuss the way forward in the war with Iran.

Rubio responded to questions on high energy prices by saying they would be “double” if Iran had a nuclear weapon.

“And they would use that nuclear weapon to control the Straits of Hormuz forever. They would be able to choke off the world’s energy supply any time they wanted,” Rubio said.

The Trump administration has given conflicting statements on their reasons for starting the war with Iran, having claimed that Iran was a short time away from building a nuclear weapon while also boasting of having obliterated Iran’s nuclear program in strikes carried out in June 2025. Rubio, at the start of the war, said the U.S. joined Israel in striking Iran to preempt Iranian retaliation against American military sites in the region.

articles.title: Trump needs to be bold, direct with Xi over Taiwan dispute
articles.summary: As Trump’s prospects for electoral redemption seemingly sink into oblivion, his negotiating position confronting Xi on trade and Taiwan are at the vanishing point.
articles.body:
U.S.-China summit meetings always have the potential for major developments, with historic international consequences. This week’s discussion in Washington between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping promises to be more consequential than most. That it is being held in D.C. rather than Beijing is a small blessing for the U.S. national interest and for long-term international security.

U.S. presidents have tended to ingratiate themselves with adversarial Chinese hosts by making ill-advised, gratuitous concessions to China regarding Taiwan’s fate. Richard Nixon in 1972 set the stage for formal de-recognition of Taiwan in the Shanghai Communiqué, officially consummated by Jimmy Carter. Bill Clinton, despite having been advised not to do so, announced the “three nos” during his June 1998 visit to China: no U.S. support for Taiwan independence, no “Two Chinas” policy and no support for Taiwan’s official participation in international organizations.

Having the meeting on America’s home turf just weeks before the midterm elections should give a small negotiating advantage to Trump. Though marginal, it is better than providing even a slight edge to Chinese hosts who know how to exploit it over the long run. But then Trump could squander his home-court advantage if he appears over-eager, even desperate, for a negotiating “win” to boost sagging Republican prospects in November .

While achieving a “successful” trade deal will be a paramount objective for Trump , Xi will surely seek some rhetorical concession that can be seen as softening the U.S. strategic and moral commitment to Taiwan’s defense . That possibility, conveying weakness in the face of Xi’s dominance, could damage Trump politically even further.

Xi has already laid the groundwork for such a scenario with his and his subordinates’ explicit warnings to the U.S. president to tread carefully on the Taiwan issue. It is noteworthy that Trump has never responded in kind to such implied threats, instead insisting that he and Xi have a “ great ” and “ friendly ” relationship. This echoes the things Trump said about Xi’s good intentions during the COVID pandemic ; only when it was obvious to all that Xi had deceived him about the growing danger to Americans, at the eventual cost of a million U.S. lives , did he publicly admit to being a little “ unhappy ” with his supposedly friendly Chinese interlocutor. But Xi soon deployed his ego-massaging weapons, and in Trump’s second term all is now forgiven .

Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice …

As Trump’s prospects for electoral redemption seemingly disappear , his negotiating position confronting Xi on trade and Taiwan are also diminishing. Xi knows this, and could offer Trump a modest trade victory in exchange for some innocent-sounding language on Taiwan — e.g., that both China and the U.S. will cease sending weapons or forces to the Taiwan Strait to avoid the kind of confrontation that is now interfering with free navigation in the Gulf of Hormuz . Trump should reject any such offer, and seriously consider hurling a “Hail Mary” of his own.

Once Xi has landed in Washington, Trump should let it leak out that he intends to propose a bold resolution of the Taiwan issue that will restore peace and security to the region. In his welcoming remarks, he should call upon Xi to renounce permanently the use of force by China against Taiwan, in exchange for Taiwan’s pledge not to declare formal independence for the next 10 years or until Xi leaves office, whichever occurs later. In all other respects, Taiwan will retain its de facto independence and democratic system, with full U.S. military backing.

Trump should commit the U.S. not only to defend Taiwan but to recognize its independence immediately upon Chinese exercise of force against it. In doing so, he will defy China’s threat that “ independence means war ” and declare instead the reverse: war means independence. The explicit commitment will eliminate once and for all Washington’s policy of strategic ambiguity that was first articulated by the Clinton administration.

Joseph Bosco served as China country director for the secretary of Defense from 2005 to 2006 and as Asia-Pacific director of humanitarian assistance and disaster relief from 2009 to 2010. He is a nonresident fellow at the Institute for Corean-American Studies, a member of the advisory board of the Global Taiwan Institute and member of the advisory board of the Vandenberg Coalition.

articles.title: Burberry isn’t a nostalgia brand, it’s a heritage brand
articles.summary: How can a 170-year-old brand feel modern? The answer may lie in understanding the difference between building on heritage versus leaning on nostalgia.
articles.body: How can a 170-year-old brand feel modern? The answer may lie in understanding the difference between building on heritage versus leaning on nostalgia. At the Burberry show on Monday night — the final event on the London Fashion Week calendar — Britain’s oldest luxury fashion brand, under the creative stewardship of designer Daniel Lee, showed it can still build. The new collection, created in collaboration with the exuberant, swinging sixties textile designer Celia Birtwell, featured happy prints: embellished and texturized floral motifs of bright yellow mimosas and twisting vines jazzing up the bright white box tent outside the Chelsea College of Arts. Silhouettes were slouchy, and washed silk and cotton fabrics made the clothing feel fresh and easy to slip into. These clothes are meant for spring, so the practicality of the Burberry brand was rendered though layered looks that offered the agility needed to live through three months of April showers. With Birtwell’s influence, the classic and sometimes harsh Burberry check was made more gentle, closer to a subtle gingham. But she also introduced some more off-kilter fun with a series of looks featuring garish, smiley faces dug up from her own archive. Backstage after the show, Lee talked about how buying is about chasing a feeling. We don’t need a mimosa-adorned shift skirt, after all, but we might really want one. A luxury garment is “not a necessity product,” he said. “It’s an emotional thing,” explaining that he wanted clothes to look worn and imperfect this season. Softer interpretations of the trench were ruched, pouffed and purposefully wrinkled. The 40-year-old designer is part of a whole class of millennials working for historical fashion houses who have been tasked with making young shoppers feel things. The designers and brands succeeding right now appear to be those who understand how to honor history and invigorate the brand, without being held back or weighed down by legacy. Matthieu Blazy (42) is doing this in the most refreshing and exciting way at Chanel. Jonathan Anderson’s (41) Dior is also working because he understands how to triangulate historical curation with modern design and artful references. Ultimately, the heritage brands that are selling clothes, offer you reliable provenance while also making you excited for what’s to come. Matthew Rider (45) at Celine gets it, too, and there’s a lot of interest in what 35-year-old Grace Wales Bonner will do with menswear at Hermès when she shows her first collection for the luxury French house next year. Issues arise when brands and their designers can’t figure out how to move beyond their heyday. Perhaps this is why beloved ‘90s nostalgia brands like McQueen and Calvin Klein (both with sliding revenues) aren’t resonating as well. It’s difficult to separate McQueen from the genius of its founder Alexander and his tragic death. The task of respecting that important chapter in fashion history while driving the brand forward may be an impossible one. Choosing to leave Paris and show in London, as the brand did this season, made sense and certainly generated excitement. But it’s unclear if the collection did more than give Londoners and McQueen loyalists a nostalgic night out. Calvin Klein, meanwhile, has struggled to keep a firm enough grasp on its own heritage and narrative. Calvin Klein wrote the playbook on a form of minimalism that other designers like the Row, Khaite and Toteme arguably do better now, reducing the brand to a reference on Carolyn Bassette-Kennedy moodboards. But with campaigns romanticizing the British countryside and a new mini exhibition at London’s Victoria and Albert Museum honoring one of its greatest hallmarks, the trusty trench, Burberry is fully owning its history. It’s also true that Lee and the team around him are thinking about how to weave some surprises and a little delight into well-made utilitarian staples. It’s this combined approach which is making more people want to buy the clothes (retail sales are up 5%, which in a challenging luxury market isn’t nothing) and making a very old brand feel young.

articles.title: Netanyahu may have ignored a dire warning. Israel ignores the deeper threat.
articles.summary: Israel risks drifting back into an Oct. 6 reality: a contained, managed Hamas quietly rebuilding behind a calm facade, primed to explode again.
articles.body:
Israelis are still debating whether the recent report is true — whether the United Arab Emirates warned Israel of an imminent Hamas attack roughly 10 days before the Oct. 7 massacre.

But fixating on the few days before Oct. 7 obscures a deeper flaw: The Israeli mindset, the strategic conception , remains largely unchanged. It is conflict management. Israel is a weakened and deterred Hamas ruling Gaza as an excuse to deepen the divide between Gaza and a Palestinian Authority-run West Bank. By avoiding allowing any alternative to emerge, it is sidelining the Palestinian question altogether.

If the deadliest disaster of Jews since the Holocaust should have changed one thing, it was this. Yet, strip away the rhetoric of “ total victory ,” and Israel’s Gaza policy today looks quite similar, just with more bloodshed and rubble.

In recent weeks, Israeli leaders have vowed to remain in Gaza for the long term and end Hamas’s rule once and for all. Following a string of successful assassinations of Hamas commanders, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz declared : “Our message is clear: No terrorist is immune, and Hamas will not be in Gaza.”

Weakening Hamas is legitimate, and so is Israel’s demand that it relinquish control of Gaza. But Israel’s revealed preference tells a different story.

Even as Israel holds an estimated 60 percent of Gaza , Hamas still controls over 95 percent of the population. Hamas is both a terrorist organization and Gaza’s de facto government; removing the former requires an alternative for the latter. Israel refused to hand that role to the Palestinian Authority but signed on to President Trump’s 20-point plan last year, which offers exactly that: a transition to the technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, eventually leading to a reformed Palestinian Authority.

The Israeli government apparently never intended to let that alternative emerge.

Members of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza remain in Cairo, with no timeline for entering Gaza. Roughly 6,000 vetted police recruits, meant to begin training months ago, have not left Gaza because Israel will not commit to letting them return.

Construction of a base for the International Stabilization Force is stalled by bureaucracy. Reconstruction of the Israeli-held “Green Zone” meant to showcase non-Hamas governance hasn’t advanced. And in the West Bank, Israeli policy is weakening the Palestinian Authority toward collapse and carving the territory into cantons to ensure no Palestinian governance, with or without Gaza, is ever viable.

Hamas has expectedly stalled the plan too. But in August it accepted the Board of Peace’s roadmap, listing 15 principles for phased disarmament in exchange for Israel Defense Forces withdrawal. Israel has valid concerns, including the roadmap’s timeline, scope of disarmament and Qatar and Turkey’s role in verifying compliance.

But justified skepticism does not excuse refusing to engage. Instead of making Hamas back its words, Israel has effectively handed it veto power over the process, drawing international blame for stalling while Hamas gains recognition as a legitimate partner.

Domestic politics explains much of this. Israel faces a charged election on Oct. 27 , and Netanyahu’s coalition cannot show compromise on Gaza. Even pressure from Trump plays in his favor, as he claims to be the only one who can stand up to who he called “the greatest friend that the state of Israel has ever had in the White House.” Netanyahu’s rivals, meantime, are trying to outflank him from the right, vowing to keep fighting rather than engage the U.S.-led plan.

But whoever wins will still have to pick up the Trump framework. The alternatives — renewed full-scale war or a Gaza permanently split between an Israeli-held east and Hamas-run west — serve neither Israel’s security interests nor produce an acceptable status quo.

Rather than campaigning on the same hawkish instinct, prime minister contenders should say that the current approach only keeps Hamas in power: deterred, but not replaced, with no real alternative given a chance.

A future Israeli government that wants a different outcome will have to act like it. This means setting a political horizon instead of managing the conflict incident by incident, taking initiative on the Trump plan and disarmament roadmap instead of being dragged along by Washington, Cairo, or Doha.

It also requires letting the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza function and supporting Palestinian Authority reform rather than treating its flaws as a pretext for exclusion and redirecting Gaza’s financial lifelines to starve Hamas economically rather than merely bombing it.

Such a shift could unlock the funding, troops and regional cooperation the plan needs, and begin restoring Israel’s ties with Europe and the Arab world.

A new government will find it hard to change course quickly. The only way to make that happen is U.S. leadership from the top, because whoever wins will want Trump on their side.

The ceasefire, the hostages’ return and the 20-point framework a year ago were a major achievement. The Trump administration can use this anniversary and Israel’s election to press ahead. Otherwise, Israel risks drifting back into an Oct. 6 reality: a contained, managed Hamas quietly rebuilding behind a calm facade, primed to explode again.

Shira Efron is the Israel policy chair and a senior fellow at RAND.

articles.title: Cuba walks out of UN General Assembly as Trump says ‘freedom will be coming’
articles.summary: The Cuban delegation to the United Nations General Assembly walked out during President Trump’s speech to the global body Tuesday after the president called for freedom on the island. Trump said “freedom will be coming to Cuba,” and accused the Cuban communist regime of fomenting opposition in the U.S. “My administration is also seeking a…
articles.body:
The Cuban delegation to the United Nations General Assembly walked out during President Trump’s speech to the global body Tuesday after the president called for freedom on the island.

Trump said “freedom will be coming to Cuba,” and accused the Cuban communist regime of fomenting opposition in the U.S.

“My administration is also seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba, where the communist regime is under great pressure — the biggest pressure they’ve ever been under. It’s an absolutely failed state,” Trump said.

“It’s failing like never before, and it will fall,” he added.

Trump imposed an effective oil blockade against Cuba beginning in January, cutting off the island from its access to Venezuelan oil after the U.S. captured Venezuela’s authoritarian leader Nicolas Maduro.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is leading negotiations with Cuban officials, although the details of the U.S. demands are not explicitly known, but include economic reforms and release of political prisoners.

Talks, however, have stalled and the Trump administration has ratcheted up sanctions against entities related to Cuba’s military and communist regime.
